    5. Commonly Used Java Classes

    Here we present a few frequently used classes from the Java platform: strings, arrays, collections, files, and regular expressions. We also include the API Stream (Java 8), which is currently the most common way to search, sort, group, or transform elements in a Java collection. Before that, we’ll show you how to find information about the thousands of available classes. This resource is indispensable for any Java developer, even experienced ones.

    With the exception of two (the JSON example and the sample application at the end), the examples in this chapter are compact source files executed by the source code launcher: [java Fichier.java]. They are located in the [05-classes-java] folder of the course code and run, like the entire course, in French (locale fr-FR). Note that a compact source file automatically imports all public classes from the [java.base] module: [java.util], [java.io], [java.nio.file], [java.util.regex], [java.util.stream], [java.time]… This is why the programs below do not contain any [import] statements.

    5.1. Seeking Help with Java Classes

    The Java Standard Library (the API Java SE) includes more than 4,000 public classes. No one knows them all: Java developers constantly consult their documentation. This documentation is available online, free of charge, and published for each version of Java.

    5.1.1. Online Documentation

    The starting point is Oracle’s website at docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25. There you’ll find:

    • the Java 25 reference: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/. It describes, module by module and package by package, all Java classes and interfaces: their constructors, fields, and methods;
    • a search box at the top of each page of the reference, where you can type the name of a class or method ([StringBuilder], [Matcher.find]…): the list of results populates as you type;
    • the Java language specification (JLS) and topic-specific guides (JDK tools, security, regular expressions…);
    • a “New Features” page that describes what’s new in each version. The new features themselves are described by JEP (JDK Enhancement Proposals), available on openjdk.org/jeps: For example, JEP 512 describes the compact source files used in this chapter.

    A class page, such as java.lang.String, provides:

    • the class’s module and package;
    • its declaration, its parent classes, and the interfaces it implements;
    • a general description, often lengthy and detailed, with examples;
    • a summary list of its fields, constructors, and methods, followed by details for each: parameters, return value, possible exceptions, and the Java version in which it was introduced (under the “Since” heading).

    The documentation is in English. A search on a search engine using the class’s full name and version (“java.lang.StringBuilder 25”) usually leads directly to the correct page.

    5.1.2. Javadoc and the editor’s help

    This documentation is generated by the [javadoc] tool from the JDK tool based on the documentation comments written in the source code of the classes. Such a comment begins with [/**] and is placed immediately before a class, field, or method. For example, here is the tax calculation method from the sample application in this chapter, documented as follows:

        /**
     * Calcule l'impôt d'un contribuable.
     *
     * @param marie     vrai si le contribuable est marié
     * @param nbEnfants nombre d'enfants
     * @param salaire   salaire annuel en euros
     * @return le montant de l'impôt, en euros
     */
    int calculer(boolean marie, int nbEnfants, int salaire);

    The comment begins with a summary sentence; the [@param] tags describe the parameters, and [@return] describes the returned value ([@throws] would describe an exception). You can document your own code in this way; the command [javadoc] (or [mvn javadoc:javadoc] in a Maven project) generates HTML pages similar to those in Java. Starting with Java 23, documentation comments can also be written in Markdown, with lines beginning with [///].

    The code editor (IntelliJ IDEA, Visual Studio Code with the Extension Pack for Java) leverages these comments and provides immediate assistance without leaving the code:

    • autocompletion: after typing [uneChaine.], the editor displays a list of the object’s methods, along with their parameters and return types;
    • Quick documentation: Hovering over a class or method name (or pressing Ctrl+Q in IntelliJ IDEA) displays its Javadoc;
    • Parameter help: When you type the opening parenthesis of a call (or press Ctrl+P in IntelliJ IDEA), the editor displays the different method overloads and the role of each parameter;
    • Go to Definition (Ctrl+B in IntelliJ, IDEA, F12 in VS Code): displays the source code for the class or method. JDK comes with the source code for its entire library (file [lib/src.zip]): This allows you to read the code for [ArrayList] or [HashMap], written by top Java experts, which is very educational.

    Finally, the [jshell] tool from JDK lets you test a method without writing a program: you enter an expression, and it displays its value. Thus, ["abc".repeat(3)] displays ["abcabcabc"]. The command [/help] from [jshell] lists its options.

    5.2. Strings

    5.2.1. The String class

    The [String] type ([java.lang] package) represents character strings. It offers numerous methods. Here are a few of them:

    Method
    role
    [int length()]
    number of characters in the string
    [char charAt(int index)]
    Character No. [index]; the first character is No. 0
    [boolean startsWith(String prefix)]
    returns [true] if the string begins with [prefix]
    [boolean endsWith(String suffix)]
    returns [true] if the string ends with [suffix]
    [boolean contains(CharSequence s)]
    returns [true] if the string contains [s]
    [boolean equals(Object autre)]
    returns [true] if the string has the same content as [autre]; [equalsIgnoreCase] is case-insensitive
    [int indexOf(String str)]
    the first occurrence of [str] in the string, or -1. Another overload starts the search at position [fromIndex]
    [int indexOf(int ch)]
    same for the character [ch]
    [int lastIndexOf(int ch)]
    same as [indexOf] but returns the last position instead of the first
    [static String join(CharSequence delimiter, CharSequence... elements)]
    Class method: concatenates the elements, separating them with [delimiter]
    [String replace(char oldChar, char newChar)]
    returns a copy of the string where the character [oldChar] has been replaced by [newChar]; an overload replaces one string with another
    [String[] split(String regex)]
    the string is treated as a sequence of fields separated by a separator described by the regular expression [regex]; the result is an array of these fields
    [String substring(int beginIndex, int endIndex)]
    substring consisting of the characters from position [beginIndex] (inclusive) to position [endIndex] (exclusive)
    [String toLowerCase()], [String toUpperCase()]
    converts the string to lowercase, uppercase
    [String strip()]
    removes leading and trailing spaces from the string (Java 11; [stripLeading], [stripTrailing]: on one side only)
    [String repeat(int count)]
    repeats the string [count] times (Java 11)
    [boolean isEmpty()], [boolean isBlank()]
    returns [true] if the string is empty, or if it contains only spaces (Java 11)
    [Stream<String> lines()]
    returns the lines of the string as a stream (Java 11; see API Stream below)
    [String formatted(Object... args)]
    returns the string, used as a template, in which the placeholders [%s], [%d]… have been replaced by the arguments (Java 15)

    It is important to note that a string of type [String] is immutable; it cannot be modified after it is created. When a method returns a string, that string is different from the string on which the method was applied. Thus, [s1.strip()] returns the string [s2], and [s1] and [s2] are two different strings: [s1] has not changed.

    Unlike in other languages, a Java string is not an array: you do not write [c[i]] but [c.charAt(i)], and the number of characters is obtained using the [c.length()] method (with parentheses, whereas the length of an array is the [tableau.length] field, without parentheses).

    // some methods of the String class
void main() {
    String uneChaine = "l'oiseau vole au-dessus des nuages";
    affiche("uneChaine=" + uneChaine);
    affiche("uneChaine.length()=" + uneChaine.length());
    affiche("uneChaine.charAt(10)=" + uneChaine.charAt(10));
    affiche("uneChaine.indexOf(\"vole\")=" + uneChaine.indexOf("vole"));
    affiche("uneChaine.indexOf(\"x\")=" + uneChaine.indexOf("x"));
    affiche("uneChaine.lastIndexOf('a')=" + uneChaine.lastIndexOf('a'));
    affiche("uneChaine.lastIndexOf('x')=" + uneChaine.lastIndexOf('x'));
    affiche("uneChaine.substring(4, 11)=" + uneChaine.substring(4, 11));
    affiche("uneChaine.toUpperCase()=" + uneChaine.toUpperCase());
    affiche("uneChaine.toLowerCase()=" + uneChaine.toLowerCase());
    affiche("uneChaine.replace('a', 'A')=" + uneChaine.replace('a', 'A'));
     // No insert method: concatenate two substrings
    affiche("insertion de \"ne \" en position 9=" + uneChaine.substring(0, 9) + "ne "
            + uneChaine.substring(9));
     // Splits the string into words (separator: a sequence of spaces)
    String[] champs = uneChaine.split("\\s+");
    for (int i = 0; i < champs.length; i++) {
        affiche("champs[" + i + "]=[" + champs[i] + "]");
    }
    affiche("String.join(\":\", champs)=" + String.join(":", champs));
    affiche("\"  abc  \".strip()=[" + "  abc  ".strip() + "]");
     // the original string has not been modified
    affiche("uneChaine=" + uneChaine);
}

// a display method
void affiche(String msg) {
    IO.println(msg);
}

    Comments:

    • line 6: character #10, i.e., the 11th character in the string;
    • Lines 8, 10: An unsuccessful search returns -1;
    • Line 11: The two parameters of [substring] are the positions of the first protected character and the first unprotected character: this yields the 7 characters at positions 4 through 10. This is the general Java convention for specifying an index range (start included, end excluded): it appears in many methods;
    • Lines 16–17: The [String] class does not have an insertion method: we concatenate the beginning of the string, the inserted text, and the end of the string. We’ll see that the [StringBuilder] class has a [insert] method;
    • Line 19: [split] splits the string into fields. Its parameter is not a single character but a regular expression, which we’ll examine at the end of the chapter: ["\\s+"] denotes a sequence of one or more whitespace characters (space, tab, line break, etc.). The character [\] must be doubled in a Java string, hence the notation [\\s];
    • line 23: the static method [join] performs the inverse of [split];
    • line 24: [strip] (Java 11) removes leading and trailing spaces. There is also the older method [trim], which recognizes only the spaces in the code for ASCII; [strip] recognizes all Unicode spaces and should be preferred;
    • line 26: all of the previous methods returned new strings: [uneChaine] remained unchanged (line 21 of the results);
    • Lines 30–32: a method from the compact source file, called by the method [main] as in Chapter 3.

    // split and join
void main() {
    String ligne = "un:deux::trois:";
     // splitting using the separator ':'
    String[] champs = ligne.split(":");
    for (int i = 0; i < champs.length; i++) {
        IO.println("champs[" + i + "]=[" + champs[i] + "]");
    }
     // The reverse operation does not restore the original string: the final empty field is missing
    IO.println("join=[" + String.join(":", champs) + "]");

     // With a negative limit, split preserves the empty fields at the end
    champs = ligne.split(":", -1);
    IO.println("split(\":\", -1) : " + champs.length + " champs, join=[" + String.join(":", champs) + "]");

     // The separator is a regular expression: ":+" matches a sequence of ':'
    champs = ligne.split(":+");
    IO.println("split(\":+\") : " + champs.length + " champs [" + String.join("|", champs) + "]");

     // multiple delimiters and removal of spaces around fields
    String personne = " dupont , jean ;  45 ";
    champs = personne.strip().split("\\s*[,;]\\s*");
    IO.println("split(\"\\\\s*[,;]\\\\s*\") : " + champs.length + " champs ["
            + String.join("|", champs) + "]");

     // removes spaces and empty fields, field by field
    String liste = "  rouge ,, vert ,  , bleu ";
    List<String> couleurs = new ArrayList<>();
    for (String champ : liste.split(",")) {
        String couleur = champ.strip();
        if (!couleur.isEmpty()) {
            couleurs.add(couleur);
        }
    }
    IO.println("strip + isEmpty : " + couleurs.size() + " champs [" + String.join("|", couleurs) + "]");

     // a separator containing special characters from regular expressions
    String texte = "pomme | poire | abricot";
    champs = texte.split(Pattern.quote(" | "));
    IO.println("Pattern.quote : [" + String.join(", ", champs) + "]");

     // join accepts only strings: integers must first be converted
    int[] nombres = {1, 2, 3, 4};
    String[] textes = new String[nombres.length];
    for (int i = 0; i < nombres.length; i++) {
        textes[i] = String.valueOf(nombres[i]);
    }
    IO.println("join sur des entiers : " + String.join(" + ", textes));
}

    > java Chaines02.java
champs[0]=[un]
champs[1]=[deux]
champs[2]=[]
champs[3]=[trois]
join=[un:deux::trois]
split(":", -1) : 5 champs, join=[un:deux::trois:]
split(":+") : 3 champs [un|deux|trois]
split("\\s*[,;]\\s*") : 3 champs [dupont|jean|45]

    Comments:

    • Line 5: The fields are separated by the character [:]. Two consecutive [:] characters delimit an empty field (line 4 of the results). But be careful: [split] removes empty fields from the end. The final [:] in the string delimits a fifth, empty field that has been removed: only 4 fields are obtained, and [join] does not reconstruct the original string (line 6 of the results). This is a common pitfall;
    • line 13: the second parameter of [split] is a limit. A negative limit instructs the program to keep all fields, including the empty fields at the end: we do indeed get 5 fields, and [join] reconstructs the original string;
    • line 17: Since the separator is a regular expression, we can define complex separators: [":+"] matches one or more consecutive [:] characters. The two consecutive [:]s form a single separator, and the empty field disappears;
    • Line 22: The pattern [\\s*[,;]\\s*] matches a comma or semicolon, preceded and followed by any number of spaces: the spaces surrounding the separators are removed along with them. Those at the beginning and end of the string are removed beforehand by [strip]. This produces the three “cleaned up” fields in a single statement;
    • lines 27–35: To remove both the spaces around the fields and the empty fields, you can also process the fields one by one: the field consisting of two spaces between two commas becomes empty after [strip] and is not retained. The list [ArrayList] used here to store the retained fields will be discussed a little later. We will also see that the API stream allows this processing to be written in a single instruction;
    • line 39: the [" | "] separator contains the character [|], which has a special meaning in a regular expression (“or”). The [Pattern.quote] method converts any string into a regular expression that literally matches it. We’ll use it whenever a separator contains one of the characters [\ ^ $ . | ? * + ( ) [ ] { }];
    • Lines 43–48: [join] accepts only strings (more precisely, [CharSequence] objects, an interface implemented by [String] and [StringBuilder]): an array of integers must first be converted to an array of strings. We will see that with the API Stream, [Arrays.stream(nombres).mapToObj(String::valueOf).collect(Collectors.joining(" + "))] does the same thing in a single instruction.

    5.2.3. Searching for and Comparing Strings

    String comparison is more subtle than it seems: should uppercase and lowercase letters be distinguished? How should “student” be compared to “essay”? And most importantly, in Java, what does the [==] operator compare? The program [Chaines03.java] demonstrates the search and comparison methods:

    // search for and compare strings
void main() {
    String titre = "Apprentissage du langage Java 25";

     // contains, startsWith, endsWith: exact comparison
    IO.println("contains(\"langage\") : " + titre.contains("langage"));
    IO.println("contains(\"LANGAGE\") : " + titre.contains("LANGAGE"));
    IO.println("startsWith(\"Apprentissage\") : " + titre.startsWith("Apprentissage"));
    IO.println("endsWith(\"25\") : " + titre.endsWith("25"));

     // case-insensitive: strings are compared in lowercase
    String cherche = "LANGAGE";
    IO.println("toLowerCase().contains(cherche.toLowerCase()) : "
            + titre.toLowerCase().contains(cherche.toLowerCase()));
     // regionMatches (ignoreCase, start, other, start in other, length)
    IO.println("regionMatches(true, 0, \"apprentissage\", 0, 13) : "
            + titre.regionMatches(true, 0, "apprentissage", 0, 13));

     // equality: `equals` compares contents, `==` compares references
    String reponse = "OUI";
    String oui = new StringBuilder("ou").append('i').toString();
    IO.println("oui.equals(\"oui\") : " + oui.equals("oui"));
    IO.println("oui == \"oui\" : " + (oui == "oui"));
    IO.println("reponse.equals(\"oui\") : " + reponse.equals("oui"));
    IO.println("reponse.equalsIgnoreCase(\"oui\") : " + reponse.equalsIgnoreCase("oui"));

     // alphabetical order: by character codes or by language
    String a = "élève", b = "essai";
    IO.println("\"" + a + "\".compareTo(\"" + b + "\") : " + a.compareTo(b));
    Collator collator = Collator.getInstance(Locale.FRANCE);
    IO.println("collator.compare(\"" + a + "\", \"" + b + "\") : " + collator.compare(a, b));

     // empty or blank strings
    String vide = "";
    String blanche = "   ";
    String absente = null;
    IO.println("\"\".isEmpty() : " + vide.isEmpty());
    IO.println("\"   \".isEmpty() : " + blanche.isEmpty());
    IO.println("\"   \".isBlank() : " + blanche.isBlank());
    IO.println("absente == null || absente.isBlank() : " + (absente == null || absente.isBlank()));

     // alignment and repetition
    IO.println("[" + String.format("%8s", "abc") + "] [" + String.format("%-8s", "abc") + "] ["
            + "-".repeat(8) + "]");
}

    Comments:

    • lines 6–9: [contains], [startsWith], and [endsWith] perform an exact, character-by-character comparison: “LANGAGE” is not found;
    • lines 12–14: These methods do not have a case-insensitive variant. The simplest way to perform a case-insensitive search is to convert both strings to lowercase;
    • lines 16–17: The [regionMatches] method compares a portion of one string to a portion of another string. Its first parameter specifies whether to ignore case; the subsequent parameters are the starting position in the string, the other string, the starting position in the other string, and the number of characters to compare;
    • lines 20–25: the most important part of this program. A variable of type [String] contains a reference to a string object (Chapter 4). The operator [] compares the references: it returns [true] if the two variables refer to the same object, and not to two objects with the same content. The variable [oui] (line 21) refers to a string “yes” constructed at runtime: this is a different object from the program’s literal string “yes,” and [oui == "oui"] evaluates to [false] (line 9 of the results), even though the two strings have the same content. To compare contents, we always use the method [equals], or [equalsIgnoreCase] to ignore case, which is the correct way to test a “yes” response entered from the keyboard in uppercase or lowercase. The comparison using [] “works” sometimes, when both strings are program literals, of which Java stores only a single instance: this is what makes the error difficult to detect;
    • lines 28–31: The method [compareTo] returns a negative, zero, or positive integer depending on whether the string precedes, equals, or follows the parameter string. It compares the character codes: “élève” comes after “essai” because the code for the character é (233) is greater than that for the character e (101); here, it returns the difference between the two codes, 132. To sort words according to the rules of a language, use a [java.text.Collator] object: in French, the character “é” is grouped with “e,” and “élève” comes before “essai” (line 13 of the results). We’ll use the order defined by a [Collator] to sort words intended for a user, and [compareTo] to compare technical identifiers (file names, keys, etc.);
    • lines 34–40: [isEmpty] checks for an empty string, while [isBlank] (Java 11) checks for an empty string or one containing only spaces. A variable of type [String] can also be [null] (no string): calling a method on [null] throws a [NullPointerException] exception. Therefore, we first test for [absente == null]; thanks to the short-circuit behavior of the [||] operator, [absente.isBlank()] is not evaluated when [absente] is [null];
    • Lines 43–44: [String.format("%8s", ...)] pads a string with spaces up to a length of 8 characters, either on the left or on the right, using the format [%-8s]; [repeat] repeats a string.

    5.2.4. Formats and Text Blocks

    So far, we have built the strings to be displayed using concatenation with the [+] operator. To align values in columns, set the number of decimal places for a number, or display a date, use the [String.format] method, or the [formatted] instance method (Java 15), which does the same thing. The first parameter is a format: a string in which [%[-][largeur][.précision]conversion] specifiers indicate where and how to insert the following parameters. The [Chaines04.java] program provides examples of this, as well as the Java 15 text blocks:

    // formats, text blocks
void main() {
    String nom = "dupont";
    int age = 45;
    double salaire = 2345.678;
    double taux = 0.0525;
    LocalDateTime date = LocalDateTime.of(2026, 10, 3, 14, 5, 9);

     // simple concatenation
    IO.println(nom + " a " + age + " ans");
     // %[-]width: width > 0 right-aligned, the minus sign left-aligned
    IO.println(String.format("[%10s] [%-10s] [%5d]", nom, nom, age));
    IO.println(String.format("[%12.2f] [%-12.1f] [%,.2f]", salaire, salaire, salaire));
    IO.println(String.format("[%05d] [%X] [%,d] [%e]", age, age, 1234567, salaire));
     // the `formatted` instance method (Java 15): same result
    IO.println("%s est %s".formatted(nom, age >= 18 ? "majeur" : "mineur"));

     // currency and percentage: the NumberFormat class
    NumberFormat monnaie = NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(Locale.FRANCE);
    NumberFormat pourcentage = NumberFormat.getPercentInstance(Locale.FRANCE);
    pourcentage.setMinimumFractionDigits(2);
    IO.println("[" + monnaie.format(salaire) + "] [" + pourcentage.format(taux) + "]");

     // dates: the DateTimeFormatter class
    IO.println("[" + date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd/MM/yyyy")) + "] ["
            + date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss")) + "] ["
            + date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("EEEE d MMMM yyyy")) + "]");

     // an aligned table
    String[] produits = {"pomme", "poire", "abricot"};
    double[] prix = {2.5, 3.15, 12};
    for (int i = 0; i < produits.length; i++) {
        IO.println("%-10s|%8.2f €".formatted(produits[i], prix[i]));
    }

     // the \ character must be doubled in a string
    String chemin = "C:\\data\\cours\\infos.txt";
    IO.println(chemin);

     // text block (Java 15): delimited by """, across multiple lines
    String json = """
        {
          "nom": "dupont",
          "chemin": "C:\\data"
        }
        """;
    IO.print(json);
     // a text block with %s and %d placeholders filled by formatted
    String json2 = """
        { "nom": "%s", "age": %d }""".formatted(nom, age);
    IO.println(json2);
}

    • Numbers are formatted according to the current language, in this case French: decimal point, space as a thousands separator. This is a thin non-breaking space (character U+202F), which looks like a regular space but prevents a line break in the middle of a number; Similarly, a non-breaking space (U+00A0) precedes the € symbol and the % symbol. This will be taken into account when comparing these texts to strings written with regular spaces;
    • line 16: ["...".formatted(...)] is equivalent to [String.format("...", ...)]. A conditional expression can provide a parameter;
    • lines 19–22: Monetary amounts and percentages are formatted using [java.text.NumberFormat] objects, which are derived for a given language and country ([Locale.FRANCE]). The percentage format multiplies the value by 100;
    • lines 25–27: Dates from API and [java.time] (Java 8) are formatted using a [DateTimeFormatter] object constructed from a template: [dd] day, [MM] month, [yyyy] year, [HH] hour, [mm] minutes, [ss] seconds, [EEEE] day of the week spelled out, [MMMM] month spelled out. Be careful with case: [MM] is the month, [mm] is the minutes. The names of the days and months are those used in everyday language;
    • lines 30–34: the column widths allow data to be displayed in columns;
    • Line 37: In a string, the character [\] introduces an escape sequence ([\n], [\t], [\"]…); to obtain the character [\] itself, you must double it. Java does not have “raw” strings where [\] would be a regular character, which makes writing Windows paths and regular expressions a bit cumbersome;
    • Lines 41–46: A text block (Java 15) is delimited by three quotation marks; the text begins on the line following the opening quotation marks. It can span multiple lines and contain unescaped quotation marks. The indentation common to all lines (that of the least-indented line, counting from the closing quotation marks) is removed: the text JSON is displayed without the code margin. Escape sequences remain active here: [\] must still be doubled (line 44). Since the closing quotation marks are on their own line, the text ends with a line break: hence the use of [IO.print] on line 47 ([IO.println] would add a blank line after the closing curly brace);
    • lines 49–50: Java does not support string interpolation—that is, expressions written directly within the text, such as [${nom}] in other languages (a proposal, “String Templates,” was tested as a preview in Java 21 and 22, then removed). With a block of text, placeholders such as [%s], [%d]… are used, filled in by [formatted]. Placing the closing quotation marks at the end of the text prevents a final line break.

    There is also the class [java.text.MessageFormat], whose formats refer to parameters by their numbers: [MessageFormat.format("{0} a {1} ans", nom, age)]. It is used for messages translated into multiple languages, where the order of parameters may vary from one language to another.

    5.2.5. The StringBuilder class

    We mentioned that the methods of the [String] class that are applied to a [s1] string return another [s2] string. The [java.lang.StringBuilder] class allows you to modify a string without creating a new string for each operation. This improves performance when constructing a string through many successive additions, by avoiding the proliferation of strings with very short lifespans.

    The class supports various constructors:

    constructor
    role
    [StringBuilder()]
    creates an empty object with an initial capacity of 16 characters
    [StringBuilder(String str)]
    construct and initialize with [str]; the initial capacity is the length of [str] plus 16
    [StringBuilder(int capacity)]
    constructing an empty object with an initial capacity of [capacity] characters

    A [StringBuilder] object stores its characters in an array whose size—its capacity—is automatically adjusted as the text grows. The program [Chaines05.java] illustrates this concept of capacity:

    // size and capacity of a StringBuilder
void main() {
    StringBuilder str = new StringBuilder("test");
    IO.println("taille=" + str.length() + ", capacité=" + str.capacity());
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        str.append("test");
        IO.println("taille=" + str.length() + ", capacité=" + str.capacity());
    }
     // a StringBuilder with an initial capacity of 10
    StringBuilder str2 = new StringBuilder(10).append("test");
    IO.println("taille=" + str2.length() + ", capacité=" + str2.capacity());
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        str2.append("test");
        IO.println("taille=" + str2.length() + ", capacité=" + str2.capacity());
    }
}

    replaces character No. [index] with [ch]
    [int indexOf(String str)]
    position of [str] in the text, or -1
    [String toString()]
    converts the text into a string [String]

    // The methods of StringBuilder return the StringBuilder object itself: they can be chained
void main() {
    StringBuilder str3 = new StringBuilder("test");
    IO.println(str3.append("abCD").insert(2, "xyZT").delete(0, 2).replace(0, 2, "XY"));
     // reverse reverses the order of the characters
    IO.println(new StringBuilder("élève").reverse());

     // builds a string piece by piece
    StringBuilder lignes = new StringBuilder();
    for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
        lignes.append("ligne ").append(i).append('\n');
    }
     // String.join to add elements separated by commas
    lignes.append(String.join(", ", "a", "b", "c")).append('\n');
     // a formatted string

    lignes.append("total=%6.1f".formatted((double) total));
     // the final string

    IO.println(resultat);
    IO.println(resultat.length() + " caractères");

     // StringJoiner: separator, prefix, and suffix
    StringJoiner joiner = new StringJoiner(", ", "[", "]");
    for (String couleur : new String[]{"rouge", "vert", "bleu"}) {
        joiner.add(couleur);
    }
    IO.println(joiner);
}

    • Line 4: The modification methods return the [StringBuilder] object itself, which allows them to be chained together. Let’s follow the steps: “test” becomes “testabCD " ([append]), then “texyZTstabCD” ([insert] in position 2), then “xyZTstabCD " ([delete] for characters 0 and 1), and finally "XYZTstabCD" ([replace] for characters 0 and 1, with "XY"). Note that, unlike the [replace] method of [String], the method of [StringBuilder] does not search for text: it replaces a range of positions. [IO.println] displays the object by calling its method [toString];
    • line 6: [reverse] reverses the text. Since [String] does not have a [reverse] method, this is the standard way to reverse a string;
    • lines 9–12: constructing a multi-line text through successive additions—this is the typical use of [StringBuilder]. The additions are chained together on a single line of code;
    • line 14: [StringBuilder] has no equivalent to [join]: the result of [String.join] is appended;
    • line 17: a formatted string is added. The conversion [%f] requires a real number: passing the integer [total] would throw a [IllegalFormatConversionException] exception at runtime, hence the conversion [(double) total];
    • line 19: the final text is obtained as a string [String];
    • lines 24–28: the class [java.util.StringJoiner] constructs a string consisting of elements separated by a separator, with an optional prefix and suffix. [String.join] performs the same function, without a prefix or suffix.

    For a few concatenations, the [+] operator is sufficient: the compiler optimizes them. [StringBuilder] is necessary when the number of additions is large or unknown, typically within a loop: the [s = s + ...] concatenation in a loop with n iterations creates n strings and copies the entire previously constructed string in each iteration. In older code, you’ll find the [StringBuffer] class, which has the same methods as [StringBuilder] but makes them usable simultaneously by multiple threads, at the cost of some performance overhead: today, [StringBuilder] is preferred over it.

    5.2.6. Parsing a string without copying it

    Each call to [substring] creates a new string in memory. In performance-critical code (such as parsing large files or network requests), you may want to avoid these creations. Java does not have a “view of a string segment” type built into the language, but several methods operate on a portion of a string without copying it. The program [Chaines07.java] compares the two ways of parsing a line in the format “last name:first name:age”:

    // parse a string without creating substrings
void main() {
    String ligne = "dupont:jean:45";

     // with substring: each field is a new string allocated in memory
    int p1 = ligne.indexOf(':');
    int p2 = ligne.lastIndexOf(':');
    String nom = ligne.substring(0, p1);
    int age = Integer.parseInt(ligne.substring(p2 + 1));
    IO.println("substring : nom=" + nom + ", âge=" + age);

     // parseInt on a portion of the string (Java 9): no intermediate string
    age = Integer.parseInt(ligne, p2 + 1, ligne.length(), 10);
     // regionMatches compares a portion of the string to another string, without copying
    boolean du = ligne.regionMatches(0, "du", 0, 2);
    IO.println("parseInt(ligne, début, fin, base) : âge=" + age + ", le nom commence par \"du\" : " + du);

     // a view of a substring: CharBuffer.wrap does not copy characters
    CharSequence vueNom = CharBuffer.wrap(ligne, 0, p1);
    IO.println("vue : nom=" + vueNom + ", longueur de la vue=" + vueNom.length()
            + ", vueNom.charAt(0)=" + vueNom.charAt(0));

     // indexOf with a search range (Java 21): the ':' is searched for between p1+1 and the end
    IO.println("indexOf(':', p1 + 1, ligne.length())=" + ligne.indexOf(':', p1 + 1, ligne.length()));

     // a string is created only if it is truly needed
    String prenom = ligne.substring(p1 + 1, p2);
    IO.println("prénom=" + prenom);
}

    Comments:

    • lines 8–9: Each call to [substring] creates a new string, even if, as with the age, it is only used for a moment;
    • line 13: an overloaded version of [Integer.parseInt] (Java 9) parses the characters between two positions in the string, relative to the specified base (here 10), without creating a substring;
    • line 15: [regionMatches], which we’ve already encountered, compares a portion of the string to another string without copying it;
    • line 19: [CharBuffer.wrap] (package [java.nio]) returns a view of the characters from 0 to [p1] - 1 in the string: an object that does not contain a copy of the characters, but provides a way to access them. It implements the [CharSequence] interface, just like [String] and [StringBuilder]: many Java methods accept a [CharSequence] ([String.join], [contains], [append], and regular expressions, for example);
    • line 24: an overloaded version of [indexOf] (Java 21) limits the search to a range of positions;
    • line 27: a string is created only if it is actually needed.

    These techniques are optimization tools: for an ordinary program, [substring] works perfectly well. Since Java 9, the virtual machine has also been storing strings that contain only characters from the Latin-1 character set (as is the case with French text) at one byte per character instead of two (“compact strings”), which cuts the memory they occupy in half. We’ll only try to avoid copies in code that has been measured to be critical for performance.

    5.3. Arrays

    5.3.1. The Arrays Class

    Java arrays are objects, but they have no useful methods: aside from the [length] field, all operations on arrays are static methods of the utility class [java.util.Arrays]. These methods allow you to sort an array, search for an element in it, copy it, fill it, and so on… Almost all of them are overloaded: there is a version for each primitive type ([int[]], [double[]], [char[]]…) and a version for arrays of objects.

    method
    role
    [static int binarySearch(int[] a, int key)]
    Returns the position of [key] in [a], which must be sorted; a negative number if [key] is missing
    [static int[] copyOf(int[] original, int newLength)]
    returns a new array of [newLength] elements containing the first elements of [original], padded with zeros if necessary ([false] for Booleans, [null] for references)
    [static int[] copyOfRange(int[] original, int from, int to)]
    returns a new array consisting of the elements from [from] (inclusive) to [to] (exclusive)
    [static boolean equals(int[] a, int[] a2)]
    Returns [true] if both arrays have the same elements in the same order
    [static void fill(int[] a, int val)]
    assigns [val] to all elements of [a]; an override fills only a range of indices
    [static void sort(int[] a)]
    sorts [a] according to the natural order of its elements; an overload sorts only a range of indices; for an array of objects, an overload receives a [Comparator] that defines the order (Chapter 4)
    [static String toString(int[] a)]
    returns the elements of the array as a string [[e1, e2, ...]]; [deepToString] does the same for an array of arrays
    [static <T> List<T> asList(T... a)]
    returns a list that is a view of the array of objects [a]
    [static IntStream stream(int[] array)]
    returns a stream of the array’s elements (see the API Stream section below)

    In addition, there is the [System.arraycopy(source, debutSource, destination, debutDestination, nombre)] method, which copies elements from one array into another existing array.

    // The Arrays class: resizing, sorting, searching
void main() {
     // Reading array elements entered via the keyboard
    double[] elements = saisie();
     // Displaying the unsorted array
    affiche("Tableau non trié", elements);
     // Linear search in an unsorted array
    recherche(elements, TypeRecherche.LINEAIRE);
     // Sorting the array
    Arrays.sort(elements);
     // Displaying the sorted array
    affiche("Tableau trié", elements);
     // binary search in the sorted array
    recherche(elements, TypeRecherche.DICHOTOMIQUE);
}

// Entering array values: returns the created array
double[] saisie() {
     // Initially, the table is empty
    double[] elements = {};
     // loop for entering array elements
    while (true) {
        String reponse = lire("Elément (réel) " + elements.length + " du tableau (rien pour terminer) : ");
         // End of entry if string is empty
        if (reponse.isEmpty()) {
            break;
        }
         // check the input
        double element;
        try {
            element = Double.parseDouble(reponse);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            IO.println("Saisie incorrecte, recommencez");
            continue;
        }
         // One more element: expand the array by one slot
        elements = Arrays.copyOf(elements, elements.length + 1);
         // and add the new element to it
        elements[elements.length - 1] = element;
    }
    return elements;
}

// display array elements
void affiche(String texte, double[] elements) {
    IO.println(texte + "-".repeat(50 - texte.length()));
    for (double element : elements) {
        IO.println(element);
    }
}

// searching the array for elements entered via the keyboard
void recherche(double[] elements, TypeRecherche type) {
    while (true) {
        String reponse = lire("Elément cherché (rien pour arrêter) : ");
         // Done?
        if (reponse.isEmpty()) {
            break;
        }
         // verification
        double element;
        try {
            element = Double.parseDouble(reponse);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            IO.println("Erreur, recommencez...");
            continue;
        }
         // Searching for the element in the array
        int i = type == TypeRecherche.DICHOTOMIQUE
                ? Arrays.binarySearch(elements, element)     // sorted array
                : indexOf(elements, element);                 // arbitrary array
         // displaying the answer
        IO.println(i >= 0 ? "Trouvé en position " + i : "Pas dans le tableau (" + i + ")");
    }
}

// linear search: the Arrays class does not have a method indexOf
int indexOf(double[] elements, double element) {
    for (int i = 0; i < elements.length; i++) {
        if (elements[i] == element) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

// reading a line from the keyboard, without the surrounding spaces; "" at the end of the stream

    Comments:

    • Lines 18–42: The [saisie] method enters array elements typed from the keyboard. Since the number of elements is unknown in advance, the program starts with an empty array (line 20) and expands it by one element for each new entry (line 37). The size of a Java array is fixed at creation: [Arrays.copyOf] actually creates a new array, one element larger, and copies the elements from the old one into it. A more efficient algorithm would allocate space in groups of N elements. An array is not designed to be expanded: this scenario is better handled with a list [ArrayList], as we will see shortly;
    • line 39: the last element of an array has the index [length - 1];
    • lines 30–35: the conversion of the entered string to a real number by [Double.parseDouble], which throws an exception [NumberFormatException] if the string is not a number. [Double.parseDouble] is not dependent on the system’s language: it always expects a decimal point and rejects the input “3,6” (line 5 of the results);
    • lines 53–75: The method [recherche] searches the array for the characters typed on the keyboard. For an unsorted array, a linear search is performed (line 71), which examines the elements one by one. The class [Arrays] does not have a method named [indexOf]: we write it (lines 78–85). For a sorted array, we perform a binary search using [Arrays.binarySearch] (line 70), which halves the search range at each step: it finds an element among one million in about twenty comparisons;
    • line 10: we sort the array. Here we use a variant of [sort] that has only one parameter: the array to be sorted. The ordering relation used to compare the array elements is then the implicit one for those elements: in this case, the natural order of numbers;
    • Lines 45–50: Displaying an array. [IO.println] displays a [double] with a decimal point, regardless of the machine’s language, and always with at least one decimal place: -7 is displayed as -7.0;
    • lines 88–91: [IO.readln] (Java 25) displays a prompt, then reads a line typed on the keyboard; it returns [null] if standard input is exhausted, for example when it comes from a file;
    • line 94: an enumeration, declared in the compact source file just like methods.

    // other methods of the Arrays class
void main() {
    int[] nombres = {40, 10, 30, 20, 50};
    affiche("nombres", Arrays.toString(nombres));

     // outputs a portion of the array: elements with indices 1 through 3 (excluding 4)
    Arrays.sort(nombres, 1, 4);
    affiche("après sort(nombres, 1, 4)", Arrays.toString(nombres));

     // copies 3 elements to another array
    int[] copie = new int[5];
    System.arraycopy(nombres, 0, copie, 0, 3);
    affiche("arraycopy", Arrays.toString(copie));
     // copyOf, copyOfRange: the copy is a new array, truncated or padded with zeros
    affiche("copyOf(nombres, 7)", Arrays.toString(Arrays.copyOf(nombres, 7)));
    affiche("copyOfRange(nombres, 1, 3)", Arrays.toString(Arrays.copyOfRange(nombres, 1, 3)));

     // fill: fills the array, or part of the array, with a value
    Arrays.fill(copie, 7);
    affiche("après fill(copie, 7)", Arrays.toString(copie));
    Arrays.fill(copie, 1, 3, 0);
    affiche("après fill(copie, 1, 3, 0)", Arrays.toString(copie));

     // comparison of two arrays: == compares the references, Arrays.equals compares the contents
    int[] autre = {7, 0, 0, 7, 7};
    IO.println("copie == autre : " + (copie == autre) + ", Arrays.equals(copie, autre) : "
            + Arrays.equals(copie, autre));

     // an array of objects viewed as a list: indexOf, lastIndexOf, reverse
    String[] couleurs = {"rouge", "vert", "bleu", "vert"};
    List<String> vue = Arrays.asList(couleurs);
    IO.println("indexOf(vert)=" + vue.indexOf("vert") + ", lastIndexOf(vert)=" + vue.lastIndexOf("vert")
            + ", indexOf(noir)=" + vue.indexOf("noir"));
     // the list is a view of the array: reversing the list reverses the array
    Collections.reverse(vue);
    affiche("après reverse", Arrays.toString(couleurs));

     // sorting an array of strings: order of character codes
    String[] mots = {"essai", "Zoé", "élève", "abricot"};
    Arrays.sort(mots);
    affiche("mots triés", Arrays.toString(mots));
     // sorting according to French language rules
    Arrays.sort(mots, Collator.getInstance(Locale.FRANCE));
    affiche("mots triés (Collator)", Arrays.toString(mots));

     // A two-dimensional array is an array of arrays
    int[][] matrice = new int[2][3];
    matrice[1][2] = 5;
    IO.println("matrice.length=" + matrice.length + ", matrice[0].length=" + matrice[0].length
            + ", deepToString=" + Arrays.deepToString(matrice));
}

// Displaying text and an array on a single line
void affiche(String texte, String tableau) {
    IO.println("%-28s: %s".formatted(texte, tableau));
}

    • Line 4: [Arrays.toString] displays a table on a single line. Displaying an array directly with [IO.println(nombres)] would result in text similar to [[I@1b6d3586]]: the type ([[I]], array of integers) and an object identifier, without its elements;

    • line 12: copies the first 3 elements of [nombres] to the beginning of [copie], while the other elements retain their initial value of 0;
    • lines 15–16: [copyOf] and [copyOfRange] create a new array. An array longer than the original is padded with zeros;
    • lines 19–22: [fill] fills the array, then resets the elements at indices 1 and 2 (excluding 3) to 0;
    • lines 25–27: As with strings, the operator [==] compares the references of two arrays, not their contents: [Arrays.equals] must be used;
    • line 31: [Arrays.asList] returns a [List] (presented in the following section), which is a view of an array of objects: it does not copy the array but provides access to it using list methods. This yields [indexOf] and [lastIndexOf] (line 32);
    • line 35: the method [Collections.reverse] reverses the order of the elements in a list. Since the list is a view of the array, it is the array itself that is reversed (line 11 of the results). The class [Arrays] does not have a reversal method; this process applies only to arrays of objects, not to arrays of primitive types such as [int[]];
    • line 40: an array of strings is sorted according to the order of the [compareTo] method described above, that is, by character codes: uppercase letters (codes 65 through 90) come before lowercase letters (97 through 122), which come before accented letters (é: 233). “Zoé” is the first word and “élève” is the last;
    • line 43: to sort according to French rules, we pass an object of type [Collator]—which is an array of strings—to [sort];
    • Lines 47–50: Java does not have two-dimensional rectangular arrays: [new int[2][3]] creates an array of 2 elements, each of which is an array of 3 integers. [matrice.length] is the number of rows, and [matrice[0].length] is the number of elements in row 0. [Arrays.deepToString] displays an array of arrays.

    The API Stream, which we will discuss later, offers other ways to search, sort, or transform the elements of an array, for example, [Arrays.stream(nombres).sum()].

    5.4. Collections

    In addition to arrays, Java provides various classes for storing collections of elements. These form the Collections Framework in the [java.util] package, which was introduced in Java 1.2 and made generic in Java 5. It is organized around interfaces, which describe what a collection does, and classes that implement them, each in its own way:

    interface
    role
    Main Implementations
    [List<E>]
    an ordered sequence of elements, accessible by their position
    [ArrayList], [LinkedList]
    [Set<E>]
    a set: no duplicates
    [HashSet], [LinkedHashSet], [TreeSet]
    [Map<K,V>]
    a dictionary: (key, value) pairs, where the keys are unique
    [HashMap], [LinkedHashMap], [TreeMap]
    [Deque<E>]
    a double-ended queue, usable as a queue or a stack
    [ArrayDeque], [LinkedList]
    [Queue<E>]
    a queue
    [ArrayDeque], [PriorityQueue]

    The interfaces [List], [Set], and [Queue] are derived from the interface [Collection<E>] ([size], [isEmpty], [contains], [add], [remove], [clear]…), which itself derives from [Iterable<E>], the interface for objects that can be iterated over using a loop [for]. Best practice is to declare variables and parameters using the interface type and to use the class name only at creation time: [List<String> villes = new ArrayList<>();]. This allows you to change the implementation without modifying the rest of the code.

    A Java collection contains only objects. Java generics do not support primitive types: you do not write [List<int>] but rather [List<Integer>], where [Integer] is the wrapper class for the type [int] (similarly, [Double] for [double], [Boolean] for [boolean]…). The compiler automatically converts a [int] to [Integer] during an assignment (“autoboxing”) and a [Integer] into a [int] during a read (“unboxing”). This conversion incurs a cost in terms of memory and time: a list of one million integers contains one million [Integer] objects. For large volumes of numbers, it is preferable to use a [int[]] array or the primitive streams ([IntStream]) introduced with the API Stream.

    The [java.util] package also contains the Java 1.0 collections: [Vector] (a list), [Hashtable] (a dictionary), and [Stack] (a stack). These are now obsolete: since they are synchronized on every operation, they are slower than their replacements [ArrayList], [HashMap], and [ArrayDeque]. They should no longer be used in new code. Similarly, avoid “raw types”—that is, generic collections used without type parameters ([List liste = new ArrayList();])—as was done before Java 5: the compiler can no longer verify the type of the added elements and issues a warning for each use.

    5.4.1. The List interface and the ArrayList class

    The class [java.util.ArrayList<E>] implements a list of objects of type [E] whose size varies during program execution. It stores its elements in an internal array that it automatically resizes, just like [StringBuilder]. Element i of a [l] list is retrieved by [l.get(i)] and modified by [l.set(i, valeur)].

    Here are some of the methods of the [List<E>] interface:

    method
    role
    [int size()]
    number of items in the list
    [boolean add(E e)]
    Adds [e] to the end of the list
    [void add(int index, E element)]
    Insert [element] at position [index] in the list
    [boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c)]
    adds the items from [c] to the end of the list
    [E get(int index)], [E set(int index, E element)]
    reads and replaces element No. [index]
    [E getFirst()], [E getLast()]
    the first and last elements (Java 21)
    [void clear()]
    deletes all elements from the list
    [boolean contains(Object o)]
    returns [true] if [o] is in the list, [false] otherwise
    [int indexOf(Object o)]
    returns the position of [o] in the list, or -1 if [o] is not found; [lastIndexOf] returns the last position
    [boolean remove(Object o)]
    deletes the first occurrence of [o]; returns [true] if the operation succeeds, [false] otherwise
    [E remove(int index)]
    deletes element No. [index] and returns
    [List<E> subList(int from, int to)]
    returns a view of the elements from [from] (inclusive) to [to] (exclusive)
    [void sort(Comparator<? super E> c)]
    sorts the list according to the order defined by [c]; [sort(null)] uses the natural order of the elements
    [<T> T[] toArray(IntFunction<T[]> generator)]
    returns the list elements as an array (Java 11)
    [static <E> List<E> of(E... elements)]
    creates an immutable list containing the given elements (Java 9)

    The utility class [java.util.Collections] complements these methods, just as [Arrays] does for arrays: [sort], [binarySearch], [reverse], [shuffle], [max], [min]…

    // The ArrayList class: the Tableaux01.java program rewritten using a list
void main() {
     // Reading list elements entered via the keyboard
    List<Double> elements = saisie();
     // number of elements
    IO.println("La liste a " + elements.size() + " éléments");
     // Displaying the unsorted list
    affiche("Liste non triée", elements);
     // linear search in the unsorted list
    recherche(elements, TypeRecherche.LINEAIRE);
     // sorting the list in natural order
    Collections.sort(elements);
     // display of the sorted list
    affiche("Liste triée", elements);
     // binary search in the sorted list
    recherche(elements, TypeRecherche.DICHOTOMIQUE);
}

// Entering values into the list: creates the list
List<Double> saisie() {
     // Initially, the list is empty
    List<Double> elements = new ArrayList<>();
     // loop for entering list items
    while (true) {
        String reponse = lire("Elément (réel) " + elements.size() + " de la liste (rien pour terminer) : ");
         // End of entry if string is empty
        if (reponse.isEmpty()) {
            break;
        }
         // Verify the entry
        double element;
        try {
            element = Double.parseDouble(reponse);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            IO.println("Saisie incorrecte, recommencez");
            continue;
        }
         // One more item in the list: it expands automatically
        elements.add(element);
    }
    return elements;
}

// generic method for displaying items in any collection
<T> void affiche(String texte, Iterable<T> elements) {
    IO.println(texte + "-".repeat(50 - texte.length()));
    for (T element : elements) {
        IO.println(element);
    }
}

// searching the list for items typed on the keyboard
void recherche(List<Double> elements, TypeRecherche type) {
    while (true) {
        String reponse = lire("Elément cherché (rien pour arrêter) : ");
         // Done?
        if (reponse.isEmpty()) {
            break;
        }
         // Verification
        double element;
        try {
            element = Double.parseDouble(reponse);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            IO.println("Erreur, recommencez...");
            continue;
        }
         // Searching for the item in the list
        int i = type == TypeRecherche.DICHOTOMIQUE
                ? Collections.binarySearch(elements, element)    // sorted list
                : elements.indexOf(element);                      // unordered list
         // displaying the answer
        IO.println(i >= 0 ? "Trouvé en position " + i : "Pas dans la liste (" + i + ")");
    }
}

// read a line from the keyboard, excluding surrounding spaces; "" at the end of the stream
String lire(String invite) {
    String ligne = IO.readln(invite);
    return ligne == null ? "" : ligne.strip();
}

// search type
enum TypeRecherche { LINEAIRE, DICHOTOMIQUE }

    Comments:

    • line 22: the list is created empty. The diamond operator [<>] (Java 7) avoids repeating the element type: the compiler infers it from the variable’s type;
    • line 39: there is no longer any need to handle list expansion; the list expands automatically. The value [element], of type [double], is automatically converted to a [Double] object;
    • line 6: the number of elements in the list. Unlike [StringBuilder], [ArrayList] does not allow you to determine its capacity; the [ensureCapacity] method only allows you to set it in advance;
    • lines 12, 70, 71: sorting and binary search are performed using the static methods [Collections.sort] and [Collections.binarySearch]; linear search using the [indexOf] method on the list, which the arrays did not have;
    • Lines 45–50: The generic method [affiche] accepts two parameters:
      • the first is the text to be written;
      • the second is an object that implements the generic interface [java.lang.Iterable<T>], whose only abstract method is [Iterator<T> iterator()].

    The loop [for (T element : elements)] is valid for any [elements] object that implements the [Iterable<T>] interface, as well as for arrays. All collections implement [Iterable]; arrays, however, do not implement it, and the [affiche] method is not suitable for an array: this is why we did not use it in [Tableaux01.java]. We will revisit this interface with the API Stream.

    // the main methods of the List interface
void main() {
     // an editable list, initialized from a non-editable list List.of
    List<String> villes = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Paris", "Lyon", "Angers"));
    affiche("départ", villes);

     // additions
    villes.add("Nantes");                       // at the end
    villes.add(1, "Brest");                     // at position 1
    villes.addAll(List.of("Lille", "Tours"));   // multiple elements at the end
    affiche("après add, add(1, ...), addAll", villes);

     // index-based access, for writing (set) and reading (get)
    villes.set(0, "Marseille");
    IO.println("get(0)=" + villes.get(0) + ", getLast()=" + villes.getLast() + ", size()=" + villes.size());

     // search
    IO.println("contains(\"Lyon\")=" + villes.contains("Lyon") + ", indexOf(\"Angers\")="
            + villes.indexOf("Angers") + ", indexOf(\"Nice\")=" + villes.indexOf("Nice"));

     // deletions
    boolean supprime = villes.remove("Lyon");   // by value
    villes.remove(0);                           // by position
    affiche("après remove(\"Lyon\") (" + supprime + "), remove(0)", villes);

     // sorting, reversal, sublist
    Collections.sort(villes);
    affiche("après sort", villes);
    Collections.reverse(villes);
    affiche("après reverse", villes);
    List<String> extrait = villes.subList(1, 3);
    affiche("subList(1, 3)", extrait);

     // conversion to array and back
    String[] tableau = villes.toArray(String[]::new);
    List<String> autre = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(tableau));
    IO.println("tableau de " + tableau.length + " éléments, nouvelle liste de " + autre.size()
            + " éléments");

     // a list of integers: remove(int) removes by position, remove(Object) by value
    List<Integer> nombres = new ArrayList<>(List.of(10, 20, 30, 1));
    nombres.remove(1);                          // removes element #1 (20)
    nombres.remove(Integer.valueOf(1));         // removes the value 1
    affiche("nombres", nombres);

     // clear clears the list
    villes.clear();
    IO.println("après clear : size()=" + villes.size() + ", isEmpty()=" + villes.isEmpty());
}

void affiche(String texte, List<?> liste) {
    IO.println("%-38s: %s".formatted(texte, liste));
}

    • line 27: the strings are sorted in their natural order, that of [compareTo];
    • line 31: [subList] returns a view of elements 1 and 2 (excluding 3), not a copy: modifying the view would modify the list;
    • lines 35–36: conversion from a list to an array, and from an array to a list. The parameter of [toArray] is a constructor reference [String[]::new], which the list uses to create an array of strings of the correct size. Method and constructor references will be covered in Chapter 7;
    • Lines 41–43: A pitfall with integer lists. The [List] interface has two methods, [remove]: [remove(int index)] deletes by position, and [remove(Object o)] deletes by value. For a [List<Integer>], [nombres.remove(1)] calls the first one and deletes element #1 (the value 20). To delete the value 1, you must pass an object [Integer]: [nombres.remove(Integer.valueOf(1))];
    • lines 47–48: [clear] clears the list; [isEmpty] checks if it is empty;
    • line 51: the type [List<?>] denotes a list of elements of any type (“wildcard,” Chapter 4): the method [affiche] accepts a [List<String>] just as it would a [List<Integer>]. A collection is displayed directly: its method [toString] returns its elements in square brackets.

    5.4.3. The Map interface and the HashMap class

    The [java.util.HashMap<K,V>] class allows you to implement a dictionary. A dictionary can be viewed as a two-column array:

    key
    value
    key1
    value1
    key2
    value2
    ...
    ...

    In the [Map<K,V>] interface, keys are of type [K], and values are of type [V]. The keys are unique: there cannot be two identical keys (as defined by the [equals] method). Such a dictionary might look like this if the types [K] and [V] referred to classes:

    A [HashMap] stores its key-value pairs in a hash table: the position of a key-value pair in the table is calculated based on the hash code of its key (method [hashCode], Chapter 4). Retrieving the value associated with a key is therefore very fast, regardless of the dictionary’s size. However, the order of the key-value pairs in the table has no relation to the order in which they were added.

    The main methods of the [Map<K,V>] interface are as follows:

    method
    role
    [int size()]
    number of (key, value) pairs in the dictionary
    [V put(K key, V value)]
    Associates [value] with [key]: adds the pair if the key is missing, otherwise replaces the value; returns the old value, or [null]
    [V putIfAbsent(K key, V value)]
    adds the key-value pair only if the key is missing; returns the existing value, or [null]
    [V get(Object key)]
    returns the value associated with [key], or [null] if the key is missing
    [V getOrDefault(Object key, V defaultValue)]
    same as above, but returns [defaultValue] if the key is missing
    [boolean containsKey(Object key)]
    returns [true] if [key] is a key in the dictionary; [containsValue] tests a value
    [V remove(Object key)]
    deletes the key-value pair [key] and returns its value, or [null]
    [Set<K> keySet()]
    all keys in the dictionary
    [Collection<V> values()]
    the collection of dictionary values
    [Set<Map.Entry<K,V>> entrySet()]
    the set of tuples in the dictionary; a tuple [Map.Entry] has the methods [getKey] and [getValue]
    [V merge(K key, V value, BiFunction<...> remappingFunction)]
    adds the pair if the key is missing; otherwise, replaces the value with the combination of the old value and [value]
    [void clear()]
    deletes all entries from the dictionary

    // the Map interface and the HashMap class
void main() {
     // creates a <String,Integer> dictionary from an array of "name:age" strings
    String[] liste = {"jean:20", "paul:18", "mélanie:10", "violette:15"};
    Map<String, Integer> dico = new HashMap<>();
    for (String element : liste) {
        String[] champs = element.split(":");
        dico.put(champs[0], Integer.parseInt(champs[1]));
    }
     // number of elements in the dictionary
    IO.println("Le dictionnaire a " + dico.size() + " éléments");
     // list of keys
    affiche("[Liste des clés]", dico.keySet());
     // list of values
    affiche("[Liste des valeurs]", dico.values());
     // List of keys and values
    IO.println("[Liste des clés & valeurs]");
    for (String cle : dico.keySet()) {
        IO.println("clé=" + cle + " valeur=" + dico.get(cle));
    }
     // the key "paul" is deleted
    IO.println("[Suppression d'une clé]");
    dico.remove("paul");
     // iterate through (key, value) pairs
    IO.println("[Liste des clés & valeurs]");
    for (Map.Entry<String, Integer> entree : dico.entrySet()) {
        IO.println("clé=" + entree.getKey() + " valeur=" + entree.getValue());
    }
     // PUT replaces the value of an existing key and returns the old value
    IO.println("put(\"jean\", 21) rend " + dico.put("jean", 21)
            + ", put(\"zoé\", 12) rend " + dico.put("zoé", 12));
     // putIfAbsent adds only if the key is missing
    IO.println("putIfAbsent(\"jean\", 22) rend " + dico.putIfAbsent("jean", 22)
            + ", get(\"jean\")=" + dico.get("jean"));
     // get returns null if the key is missing; getOrDefault returns a default value
    IO.println("get(\"x\")=" + dico.get("x") + ", getOrDefault(\"x\", -1)=" + dico.getOrDefault("x", -1)
            + ", containsKey(\"x\")=" + dico.containsKey("x"));
     // merge: adds the key with the given value, or combines the old value with the new one
    dico.merge("zoé", 1, Integer::sum);
    dico.merge("léa", 1, Integer::sum);
    IO.println("après merge : " + dico);

     // searches the dictionary
    while (true) {
        String saisie = IO.readln("Nom recherché (rien pour arrêter) : ");
        String nomCherche = saisie == null ? "" : saisie.strip();
        if (nomCherche.isEmpty()) {
            break;
        }
         // get returns the value associated with the key, or null if the key does not exist
        Integer age = dico.get(nomCherche);
        if (age != null) {
            IO.println(nomCherche + "," + age);
        } else {
            IO.println("Nom " + nomCherche + " inconnu");
        }
    }
}

// generic method to display the elements of a collection
<T> void affiche(String texte, Iterable<T> elements) {
    IO.println(texte + "-".repeat(50 - texte.length()));
    for (T element : elements) {
        IO.println(element);
    }
}

    Comments:

    • line 4: an array of strings that will be used to initialize the <String,Integer> dictionary;
    • line 5: the dictionary, which is empty;
    • lines 6–9: its initialization using the array of strings;
    • line 11: the number of key-value pairs in the dictionary;
    • lines 13–15: the keys and values of the dictionary. [dico.keySet()] and [dico.values()] are collections, so [Iterable]: the [affiche] method we’ve already encountered works here;
    • line 23: removing a pair from the dictionary;
    • Lines 26–28: A dictionary is not itself a collection, but [entrySet] returns the set of its key-value pairs, which are of type [Map.Entry<K,V>]. This approach is more efficient than the one in lines 18–20, which looks up the value of each key using [get];
    • lines 30–31: [put] adds a pair or replaces the value of an existing key, without exception or warning; the returned value—either the old value or [null]—indicates what happened;
    • lines 33–34: [putIfAbsent] does not replace the value of an existing key;
    • lines 36–37: Reading a nonexistent key does not cause an error: [get] returns [null]. [getOrDefault] allows you to choose the returned value in this case, and [containsKey] allows you to check whether a key exists;
    • Lines 39–40: [merge] adds the key “lea” with the value 1, and adds 1 to the value of the key “zoé,” which already exists. The third parameter is the function that combines the old and new values—in this case, the sum of two integers—passed as a method reference [Integer::sum] (Chapter 7). This is the standard way to count occurrences: [compteurs.merge(mot, 1, Integer::sum)];
    • lines 51–56: searching for a key in the dictionary. [get] returns a [Integer], not a [int], because it must be able to return [null]: this case is tested before the value is used. Entering [int age = dico.get(nomCherche);] would generate a [NullPointerException] for a missing key during the automatic conversion of [null] to [int].

    The keys are not listed in the order they were added, but in the order of the hash table, which depends on the keys’ hash codes: a [HashMap] does not guarantee any specific order. If the order of the keys matters, use a [LinkedHashMap], which preserves the order in which they were added, or a [TreeMap], which keeps the keys sorted: these are shown below.

    5.4.4. Other collections

    The [java.util] package contains other collections, each tailored for a specific use:

    class
    role
    [HashSet<E>]
    a set: no duplicates, no order, very fast membership test; set operations (union [addAll], intersection [retainAll], difference [removeAll])
    [LinkedHashSet<E>]
    a set that preserves the order in which its elements were added
    [TreeSet<E>]
    a set whose elements are kept sorted
    [ArrayDeque<E>]
    a double-ended queue: when used as a queue, elements are removed in the order they were added (FIFO, first in first out); when used as a stack, the last element added is the first one removed (LIFO, last in first out)
    [LinkedHashMap<K,V>]
    a dictionary that preserves the order in which its keys were added
    [TreeMap<K,V>]
    a dictionary whose keys are kept sorted
    [PriorityQueue<E>]
    a priority queue: the element that is removed is the smallest according to the queue's order
    [LinkedList<E>]
    a doubly linked list: fast insertions and deletions at the ends and during traversal

    // an overview of other collections
void main() {
     // HashSet: a set, with no duplicates and no specific order
    Set<String> langages = new HashSet<>(List.of("C#", "Java", "PHP"));
    boolean ajoute1 = langages.add("Python");
    boolean ajoute2 = langages.add("Java");             // already exists: rejected
    IO.println("HashSet : add(Python)=" + ajoute1 + ", add(Java)=" + ajoute2 + ", size()=" + langages.size()
            + ", contains(PHP)=" + langages.contains("PHP"));
    Set<String> web = Set.of("PHP", "JavaScript", "Python");
    Set<String> communs = new HashSet<>(langages);
    communs.retainAll(web);                              // intersection
    IO.println("HashSet : intersection = " + communs);
    communs.addAll(List.of("Go"));                       // union
    IO.println("HashSet : après union = " + communs);
     // TreeSet: a set whose elements are kept sorted
    IO.println("TreeSet : " + new TreeSet<>(langages));

     // ArrayDeque used as a queue: first-in, first-out
    Deque<String> file = new ArrayDeque<>();
    file.offer("client1");
    file.offer("client2");
    file.offer("client3");
    IO.println("file : peek=" + file.peek() + ", poll=" + file.poll() + ", poll=" + file.poll()
            + ", reste " + file.size());

     // ArrayDeque used as a queue: last-in, first-out
    Deque<Integer> pile = new ArrayDeque<>();
    pile.push(1);
    pile.push(2);
    pile.push(3);
    IO.println("pile : peek=" + pile.peek() + ", pop=" + pile.pop() + ", pop=" + pile.pop()
            + ", reste " + pile.size());
     // pop on an empty stack throws an exception; poll returns null
    pile.pop();
    IO.println("pile : poll sur une pile vide = " + pile.poll());
    try {
        pile.pop();
    } catch (NoSuchElementException e) {
        IO.println("pile : pop sur une pile vide : " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());
    }

     // TreeMap: a dictionary whose keys are kept sorted
    Map<String, Integer> ages = new TreeMap<>();
    ages.put("violette", 15);
    ages.put("jean", 20);
    ages.put("mélanie", 10);
    ages.put("paul", 18);
    IO.println("TreeMap : " + ages);
     // LinkedHashMap: a dictionary that preserves the insertion order of keys
    Map<String, Integer> ordre = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    ordre.put("violette", 15);
    ordre.put("jean", 20);
    ordre.put("mélanie", 10);
    IO.println("LinkedHashMap : " + ordre);

     // PriorityQueue: the element with the lowest priority is always returned
    PriorityQueue<Urgence> urgences = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingInt(Urgence::priorite));
    urgences.offer(new Urgence("entorse", 3));
    urgences.offer(new Urgence("arrêt cardiaque", 1));
    urgences.offer(new Urgence("rhume", 5));
    urgences.offer(new Urgence("fracture", 2));
    IO.print("PriorityQueue :");
    Urgence urgence;
    while ((urgence = urgences.poll()) != null) {
        IO.print(" " + urgence.patient() + " (" + urgence.priorite() + ")");
    }
    IO.println();
}

// a patient and the priority of their care
record Urgence(String patient, int priorite) {
}

    Comments:

    • line 4: a set initialized with the elements of a list;
    • line 6: [add] returns [false] if the element is already in the set, which remains unchanged;
    • Lines 9–14: [retainAll] keeps only the elements present in the other collection (intersection), while [addAll] adds those from the other collection (union). These methods modify the set: we are therefore working on a copy of [langages]. [Set.of] (Java 9) creates an immutable set. The order in which the elements of a [HashSet] are displayed has no significance;
    • line 16: a *[TreeSet]* constructed from the set displays its elements in sorted order;
    • lines 19–24: [ArrayDeque] used as a queue: [offer] inserts an element at the end of the queue, [poll] removes the oldest element, and [peek] retrieves an element without removing it. The operands of the concatenation passed to [IO.println] are evaluated from left to right: [peek], then the two [poll], then [size];
    • lines 27–32: [ArrayDeque] is used as a stack: [push] pushes an element onto the stack, and [pop] pops the most recent element. The Java 1.0 class [Stack] should no longer be used;
    • lines 34–40: on an empty stack, [pop] throws a [NoSuchElementException] exception, whereas [poll] returns [null]. Most operations of [Deque] thus exist in two versions: one throws an exception ([push], [pop], [getFirst]…), while the other returns a special value ([offer], [poll], [peek]…);
    • lines 43–48: the pairs for a [TreeMap] are listed in key order;
    • lines 50–54: those of a [LinkedHashMap] are listed in the order they were added;
    • lines 57–67: a [PriorityQueue] needs to be able to compare its elements. Here, it is passed a [Comparator] that compares priorities: [Comparator.comparingInt(Urgence::priorite)] reads “compare urgencies based on the integer value returned by their [priorite] method.” Patients are discharged in order of increasing priority, regardless of their order of arrival. The loop stops when [poll] returns [null], indicating that the queue is empty;
    • lines 71–72: A patient is represented by a [record] (Chapter 4).

    5.4.5. Immutable Collections

    A class that manages a collection often needs to expose it externally without allowing it to be modified. Java does not have a “read-only” interface distinct from [List]: a non-modifiable collection implements the full [List] interface, but its modification methods ([add], [remove], [set]…) throw a [UnsupportedOperationException] exception. There are two types:

    • non-modifiable views, obtained via [Collections.unmodifiableList(liste)] ([unmodifiableSet], [unmodifiableMap]…): they do not copy the collection but prevent recipients from modifying it;
    • The read-only collections created by [List.of(...)], [Set.of(...)], [Map.of(...)] (Java 9), or copied by [List.copyOf(collection)] (Java 10): their contents are fixed once and for all.

    // immutable collections
void main() {
    Classe classe = new Classe();
    classe.inscrire("dupont");
    classe.inscrire("martin");
     // External code can read the list of students...
    List<String> eleves = classe.getEleves();
    IO.println(eleves.size() + " élèves : " + eleves + ", get(0)=" + eleves.get(0));
     // ... but cannot modify it: the update methods throw an exception
    try {
        eleves.add("intrus");
    } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) {
        IO.println("add sur la vue : " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());
    }
    IO.println("classe de la vue : " + eleves.getClass().getName());
     // the view reflects changes made by the owning class
    classe.inscrire("durand");
    IO.println(eleves.size() + " élèves : " + eleves);

     // List.copyOf: a read-only copy that no longer sees changes made to the original
    List<String> copie = classe.getCopieEleves();
    classe.inscrire("petit");
    IO.println("copie : " + copie + ", vue : " + eleves);

     // List.of, Set.of, Map.of: immutable collections created in a single statement
    Map<String, Integer> notes = Map.of("dupont", 12, "martin", 15);
    IO.println("notes.get(\"martin\")=" + notes.get("martin") + ", containsKey(\"durand\")="
            + notes.containsKey("durand"));
    try {
        notes.put("durand", 9);
    } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) {
        IO.println("put sur Map.of : " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());
    }
     // Collections created using `of` do not accept the value `null`
    try {
        List<String> liste = List.of("a", null);
        IO.println(liste);
    } catch (NullPointerException e) {
        IO.println("List.of(\"a\", null) : " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());
    }
}

// A class that retains control of its list
class Classe {
     // The list is private: only the class can modify it
    private final List<String> eleves = new ArrayList<>();

     // A read-only view of the list
    public List<String> getEleves() {
        return Collections.unmodifiableList(eleves);
    }

     // a read-only copy of the list
    public List<String> getCopieEleves() {
        return List.copyOf(eleves);
    }

    public void inscrire(String nom) {
        eleves.add(nom);
    }
}

    Comments:

    • lines 44–61: The class [Classe] manages a list of students. The list itself is private; only the method [inscrire] allows it to be modified;
    • lines 49–51: The method [getEleves] returns a read-only view of the list. Returning the list [eleves] itself would allow external code to modify it without the class’s knowledge;
    • lines 10–14: The view has all the methods of *[List]*, and ***[eleves.add("intrus")]** is accepted by the compiler; the *[UnsupportedOperationException] exception is thrown at runtime;
    • line 15: the view’s actual class is an internal class of [Collections], which is known only through the [List] interface;
    • lines 17–18: the view does not copy the list; it sees the changes made by the owning class;
    • lines 54–56 and 21–23: [List.copyOf], on the other hand, returns a read-only copy: the list [copie] does not see the addition of “small”;
    • lines 26–33: [Map.of] creates a read-only dictionary from key-value pairs;
    • lines 35–40: The collections created by [of] and [copyOf] reject the value [null], which triggers a [NullPointerException] immediately upon their creation.

    The type of a variable such as [List<String>] therefore does not indicate whether the list is mutable: it is up to the documentation for the method that returns it to specify this. A common best practice is to return immutable collections and to create a new collection whenever you want to modify one. [record], whose fields are read-only, align well with this practice: [record Classe(String nom, List<String> eleves)] benefits from copying its list into its constructor using [List.copyOf].
