    // Sorting with a Comparator, sequenced collections, iteration, and deletion
void main() {
    List<Eleve> eleves = new ArrayList<>(List.of(
            new Eleve("martin", 15), new Eleve("dupont", 12), new Eleve("Durand", 15),
            new Eleve("élise", 9), new Eleve("petit", 12)));

     // 1 - A Comparator defines an order; its methods determine that order
    eleves.sort(Comparator.comparing(Eleve::nom));
    IO.println("par nom                  : " + noms(eleves));
    eleves.sort(Comparator.comparing(Eleve::nom, Collator.getInstance(Locale.FRANCE)));
    IO.println("par nom (Collator)       : " + noms(eleves));
    eleves.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Eleve::note).reversed()
            .thenComparing(Eleve::nom, String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER));
    IO.println("note décroissante, nom   : " + noms(eleves));

     // 2 - Sequenced collections (Java 21): first, last, reverse order
    IO.println("getFirst()=" + eleves.getFirst().nom() + ", getLast()=" + eleves.getLast().nom()
            + ", reversed()=" + noms(eleves.reversed()));
    LinkedHashSet<String> villes = new LinkedHashSet<>(List.of("Angers", "Paris", "Nantes"));
    villes.addFirst("Lyon");
    IO.println("LinkedHashSet : " + villes + ", getLast()=" + villes.getLast() + ", reversed()="
            + villes.reversed());
    TreeMap<String, Integer> notes = new TreeMap<>(Map.of("martin", 15, "dupont", 12, "petit", 12));
    IO.println("TreeMap : firstEntry()=" + notes.firstEntry() + ", lastEntry()=" + notes.lastEntry()
            + ", reversed()=" + notes.reversed());

     // 3 - Removing elements during a `for` loop: exception (trying to operate on a copy)
    List<Eleve> copie = new ArrayList<>(eleves);
    try {
        for (Eleve eleve : copie) {
            if (eleve.note() == 12) {
                copie.remove(eleve);
            }
        }
    } catch (ConcurrentModificationException e) {
        IO.println("remove dans un for : " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());
    }
     // The right way: the explicit iterator and its `remove` method...
    for (Iterator<Eleve> iterateur = eleves.iterator(); iterateur.hasNext(); ) {
        Eleve eleve = iterateur.next();
        if (eleve.note() < 10) {
            iterateur.remove();
        }
    }
    IO.println("après iterateur.remove() : " + noms(eleves));
     // ... or, more simply, removeIf
    eleves.removeIf(eleve -> eleve.note() < 15);
    IO.println("après removeIf           : " + noms(eleves));
     // forEach: an iteration expressed using a lambda
    eleves.forEach(eleve -> IO.println("  " + eleve));
}

// the names of the students in a list
List<String> noms(List<Eleve> eleves) {
    List<String> noms = new ArrayList<>();
    for (Eleve eleve : eleves) {
        noms.add(eleve.nom());
    }
    return noms;
}

They share common methods for accessing both ends: [getFirst], [getLast], [addFirst], [addLast], [removeFirst], [removeLast] ([firstEntry], [lastEntry]… for a dictionary), and the method [reversed], which returns a view of the collection in reverse order without copying it.     • lines 28–37: you must not modify a collection while iterating over it with a [for] loop: the iterator used by the loop detects the modification and throws a [ConcurrentModificationException] exception at the next element. The test is performed on a copy of the list;

    5.5. The API Stream

    The API Stream ([java.util.stream] package, Java 8) is a set of methods that allow you to process the elements of a collection as if querying a database: filtering, sorting, grouping, calculating totals, etc. A [Stream<T>] stream is a sequence of elements of type [T] that are passed through a chain of operations. It is obtained from a collection ([liste.stream()]), an array ([Arrays.stream(tableau)]), values ([Stream.of(1, 2, 3)]), rows from a file ([Files.lines(chemin)]), matches from a regular expression, and, with Hibernate (Chapter 11), rows from a database table.

    These streams should not be confused with the input-output streams ([InputStream], [OutputStream]) that we will encounter with files: these are two unrelated concepts.

    5.5.1. The Iterable and Iterator Interfaces

    Before introducing streams, let’s revisit the [Iterable<T>] interface, which applies to objects that are iterated over using a [for] loop. It contains only one abstract method, [iterator], which returns an iterator [Iterator<T>]: an object that indicates whether there are any remaining elements ([hasNext]) and returns the next element ([next]).

    An object [Iterable] does not need to contain its elements: its iterator can generate them one by one, on demand. The program [Streams01.java] provides an example of this and presents an infinite stream:

    // the Iterable and Iterator interfaces; an infinite stream
void main() {
     // 1 - a `for` loop over an `Iterable` object that yields its elements on demand
    IO.println("[for sur new Pairs(6)]");
    for (int n : new Pairs(6)) {
        IO.println("  reçu " + n);
    }

     // 2 - what the `for` loop does: it requests an iterator from the `Iterable` object
    IO.println("[itération à la main]");
    Iterable<Integer> sequence = new Pairs(4);
    Iterator<Integer> iterateur = sequence.iterator();
    while (iterateur.hasNext()) {
        IO.println("  next()=" + iterateur.next());
    }

     // 3 - an infinite stream: its elements are computed only as needed
    IO.println("[flux infini]");
    Stream.iterate(new long[]{0, 1}, f -> new long[]{f[1], f[0] + f[1]})
            .map(f -> f[0])
            .takeWhile(f -> f <= 100)
            .forEach(f -> IO.print(f + " "));
    IO.println();

     // 4 - A list is iterable, a string is not: we iterate over its characters
    Iterable<String> mots = List.of("un", "deux");
    String lettres = "abc".chars()
            .mapToObj(c -> String.valueOf((char) c))
            .collect(Collectors.joining("-"));
    IO.println("[autres séquences] " + lettres + " " + String.join("-", mots));
}

// even numbers from 0 to max, generated one by one by an iterator
record Pairs(int max) implements Iterable<Integer> {

    @Override
    public Iterator<Integer> iterator() {
        IO.println("  (début de l'itération)");
        return new Iterator<>() {
             // the next number to be generated
            private int suivant = 0;

            @Override
            public boolean hasNext() {
                boolean encore = suivant <= max;
                if (!encore) {
                    IO.println("  (fin de l'itération)");
                }
                return encore;
            }

            @Override
            public Integer next() {
                if (suivant > max) {
                    throw new NoSuchElementException();
                }
                IO.println("  (production de " + suivant + ")");
                int n = suivant;
                suivant += 2;
                return n;
            }
        };
    }
}

    • lines 34–64: The record [Pairs] implements the interface [Iterable<Integer>]: its method [iterator] returns an iterator that produces even numbers from 0 to [max]. It does not construct any list: it simply stores the next number to be generated (line 41);
    • line 39: the iterator is an anonymous class—a class without a name, declared and instantiated in a single expression [new Iterator<>() { ... }], which implements both methods of the interface. It has access to the [max] component of the record;
    • lines 44–50: [hasNext] indicates whether there is one more element to generate;
    • lines 53–61: [next] produces the next element. When called after there are no more elements, it must invoke a [NoSuchElementException];
    • lines 5–7: The results (lines 3–12) show that the production of an element by the iterator and its consumption by the [for] loop alternate;
    • lines 11–15: what the [for] loop actually does: it requests an iterator from the object, calls [hasNext] as long as that method returns [true], and obtains each element via [next];
    • lines 19–22: an infinite sequence, the Fibonacci sequence. [Stream.iterate(graine, fonction)] produces the seed, then the result of the function applied to the seed, then the result of the function applied to that result, and so on. Each element here is an array of two consecutive numbers in the sequence; [map] keeps only the first one, [takeWhile] stops the stream at the first number greater than 100, and [forEach] displays each number. The entire stream is never calculated; only the requested elements are computed;
    • Lines 26–30: A list is [Iterable]. A string is not: it cannot be iterated over directly using [for]. Its method [chars] returns the stream of its characters as integer codes, which are then converted back into single-character strings, and [Collectors.joining("-")] concatenates them with a separator. You can also iterate over the array returned by ["abc".toCharArray()].

    Java does not have a statement that allows you to define an iterator as a simple method that produces its elements one by one ([yield return] in other languages): you must either implement the iterator class, as shown here, or use the stream creation methods ([Stream.iterate], [Stream.generate]), which also produce their elements on demand. This on-demand generation mechanism is used throughout the API Stream.

    5.5.2. Filtering, Projecting, Sorting

    // the API stream: filter, map, sort
void main() {
     // the data: a list of people
    List<Personne> personnes = List.of(
            new Personne("dupont", "jean", 45, "Angers"),
            new Personne("martin", "marie", 17, "Paris"),
            new Personne("durand", "paul", 32, "Angers"),
            new Personne("leroy", "sophie", 28, "Nantes"),
            new Personne("moreau", "luc", 15, "Paris"),
            new Personne("simon", "julie", 52, "Angers"),
            new Personne("laurent", "marc", 32, "Lyon"));

     // filter: adults; p -> p.age() >= 18 is an anonymous function
    Stream<Personne> majeurs = personnes.stream().filter(p -> p.age() >= 18);
    affiche("[filter : les majeurs]", majeurs);

     // map: a projection; here, each person becomes a string
    Stream<String> noms = personnes.stream().map(p -> p.prenom() + " " + p.nom().toUpperCase());
    affiche("[map : prénom NOM]", noms);

     // the operations are chained together: the names of people from Angers, in alphabetical order
    List<String> angevins = personnes.stream()
            .filter(p -> p.ville().equals("Angers"))
            .map(Personne::nom)
            .sorted()
            .toList();
    affiche("[filter + map + sorted : les Angevins]", angevins.stream());

     // sorting by multiple criteria: age in descending order, then names in ascending order
    Stream<Personne> tries = personnes.stream()
            .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(Personne::age).reversed().thenComparing(Personne::nom));
    affiche("[sorted avec un Comparator]", tries);

     // the element’s position: we iterate through the indices using a IntStream
    Stream<String> numerotes = IntStream.range(0, 3).mapToObj(i -> (i + 1) + ". " + personnes.get(i).nom());
    affiche("[IntStream.range : numérotation]", numerotes);

     // A stream is traversed only once
    Stream<Personne> flux = personnes.stream().filter(p -> p.age() < 18);
    IO.println("[un flux déjà parcouru] " + flux.count() + " mineurs");
    try {
        flux.count();
    } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
        IO.println("  " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
    }
}

// displaying the elements of a stream
<T> void affiche(String titre, Stream<T> flux) {
    IO.println(titre);
    flux.forEach(element -> IO.println("  " + element));
}

// a person
record Personne(String nom, String prenom, int age, String ville) {
}

    Comments:

    • lines 4–11: the list of people, which cannot be modified, created by [List.of];
    • line 55: the [Personne] record. A compact source file places its type declarations next to its methods;
    • Line 14: [personnes.stream()] returns the stream of list elements. The method [filter] filters the stream: it retains only the elements that satisfy a condition. This condition is passed to it in the form of a lambda [p -> p.age() >= 18], “the function that, for a person p, returns the Boolean [p.age() >= 18].” [filter] calls this function for each person;
    • the result of [filter] is a new stream [Stream<Personne>]: the list [personnes] remains unchanged. This holds true for all operations in the API stream;
    • Lines 49–52: The [affiche] method iterates through the stream using the [forEach] operation and displays each person using the [toString] method from the record: [Personne[nom=dupont, ...]];
    • line 18: the [map] method projects each element of the stream onto a new value, in this case a string. The result is a [Stream<String>] stream;
    • lines 22–26: The operations return streams, to which other operations can be applied. Operations are often written one per line: this chain of calls reads from top to bottom like a recipe. [Personne::nom] is a method reference, a shorthand notation for the lambda [p -> p.nom()];
    • line 25: [sorted] without parameters sorts the stream according to the natural order of its elements, in this case strings;
    • line 26: [toList] (Java 16) places the elements of the stream into an immutable list. We also encounter the older syntax [collect(Collectors.toList())], which in practice returns a mutable list (a [ArrayList]), although the documentation does not guarantee this;
    • Lines 30–31: [sorted] accepts a [Comparator], constructed as in [Collections06.java]: age in descending order, then name in ascending order to distinguish between people of the same age. Durand and Laurent, who are both 32 years old, are sorted by last name (lines 23–24 of the results);
    • line 35: the streams do not provide the positions of their elements. To number them, we iterate over the indices using an integer stream [IntStream.range(0, 3)] (0, 1, 2; 3 excluded) and convert each index to a string using [mapToObj];
    • lines 39–45: A stream is single-use: once traversed by a terminal operation (here, [count], which counts the elements), it can no longer be used and triggers a [IllegalStateException]. A new stream must be requested from the collection.

    There are two types of operations in a flow: intermediate operations ([filter], [map], [sorted]…) return a new flow; terminal operations ([forEach], [toList], [count], [collect]…) traverse the stream and produce a result. A chain of operations always ends with a terminal operation. Unlike other languages, Java does not have a query syntax similar to SQL: processing is always written as a chain of method calls.

    // the API stream: quantifiers, aggregates, element selection, partitions
void main() {
    List<Personne> personnes = List.of(
            new Personne("dupont", "jean", 45, "Angers"),
            new Personne("martin", "marie", 17, "Paris"),
            new Personne("durand", "paul", 32, "Angers"),
            new Personne("leroy", "sophie", 28, "Nantes"),
            new Personne("moreau", "luc", 15, "Paris"),
            new Personne("simon", "julie", 52, "Angers"),
            new Personne("laurent", "marc", 32, "Lyon"));

     // quantifiers: anyMatch (at least one), allMatch (all), noneMatch (none)
    IO.println("anyMatch(mineur)=" + personnes.stream().anyMatch(p -> p.age() < 18)
            + ", allMatch(mineur)=" + personnes.stream().allMatch(p -> p.age() < 18)
            + ", noneMatch(Brest)=" + personnes.stream().noneMatch(p -> p.ville().equals("Brest")));

     // aggregates; mapToInt returns a stream of int, which has sum, average, min, max
    IO.println("count()=" + personnes.stream().count()
            + ", count(Angers)=" + personnes.stream().filter(p -> p.ville().equals("Angers")).count());
    double moyenne = personnes.stream().mapToInt(Personne::age).average().orElse(0);
    IO.println("sum(âge)=" + personnes.stream().mapToInt(Personne::age).sum()
            + ", average(âge)=%.2f".formatted(moyenne));
    IntSummaryStatistics stats = personnes.stream().mapToInt(Personne::age).summaryStatistics();
    IO.println("min(âge)=" + stats.getMin() + ", max(âge)=" + stats.getMax() + ", " + stats);
     // min, max with a Comparator return the element itself, in an Optional
    Optional<Personne> plusJeune = personnes.stream().min(Comparator.comparingInt(Personne::age));
    Optional<Personne> plusAge = personnes.stream().max(Comparator.comparingInt(Personne::age));
    IO.println("min(Comparator)=" + plusJeune.get().nom() + ", max(Comparator)=" + plusAge.get().nom());

     // selects an element: findFirst returns an Optional, which is empty if there is no element
    String premier = personnes.stream().findFirst().get().nom();
    String parisien = personnes.stream().filter(p -> p.ville().equals("Paris")).findFirst().get().nom();
    IO.println("findFirst()=" + premier + ", premier de Paris=" + parisien
            + ", getLast()=" + personnes.getLast().nom());
    Optional<Personne> brestois = personnes.stream().filter(p -> p.ville().equals("Brest")).findFirst();
    IO.println("Brest : isPresent()=" + brestois.isPresent() + ", map + orElse : "
            + brestois.map(Personne::nom).orElse("personne"));
    try {
         // orElseThrow requires that there be a value
        brestois.orElseThrow();
    } catch (NoSuchElementException e) {
        IO.println("Brest : orElseThrow() : " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
    }

     // distinct: removes duplicates
    List<String> villes = personnes.stream().map(Personne::ville).distinct().toList();
    IO.println("distinct(villes)=" + villes);
     // one person per city: the first one; Set.add returns false for a city that has already been encountered
    Set<String> vues = new HashSet<>();
    List<String> unParVille = personnes.stream().filter(p -> vues.add(p.ville())).map(Personne::nom).toList();
    IO.println("une personne par ville=" + unParVille);

     // subdivisions: limit, skip, takeWhile, dropWhile
    List<String> noms = personnes.stream().map(Personne::nom).toList();
    IO.println("limit(2)=" + noms.stream().limit(2).toList() + ", skip(5)=" + noms.stream().skip(5).toList());
    IO.println("skip(2).limit(2)=" + noms.stream().skip(2).limit(2).toList()
            + ", takeWhile(longueur 6)=" + noms.stream().takeWhile(n -> n.length() == 6).toList()
            + ", dropWhile(longueur 6)=" + noms.stream().dropWhile(n -> n.length() == 6).toList());

     // Gatherers.windowFixed (Java 24): splitting into fixed-size packets (pagination)
    List<List<String>> pages = noms.stream().gather(Gatherers.windowFixed(3)).toList();
    for (int i = 0; i < pages.size(); i++) {
        IO.println("page " + (i + 1) + " : " + String.join(", ", pages.get(i)));
    }
}

}

skip(2).limit(2)=[durand, leroy], takeWhile(longueur 6)=[dupont, martin, durand], dropWhile(longueur 6)=[leroy, moreau, simon, laurent]
page 1 : dupont, martin, durand
page 2 : leroy, moreau, simon
page 3 : laurent

    Comments:

    • lines 13–15: [anyMatch] returns [true] if at least one element satisfies the condition, [allMatch] if all of them satisfy it, and [noneMatch] if none of them satisfy it;
    • lines 18–19: [count] counts the elements in the stream; to count those that satisfy a condition, the stream is first filtered. For a collection, the [size] method is obviously preferable to [stream().count()];
    • lines 20–22: [mapToInt(Personne::age)] transforms the stream of people into a [IntStream], a stream of values [int], which has calculation methods: [sum], [average], [min], [max]. [average] returns a [OptionalDouble], because the average of an empty flow does not exist; [orElse(0)] provides the value to be used in this case;
    • lines 23–24: [summaryStatistics] calculates the count, sum, minimum, average, and maximum in a single pass;
    • lines 26–28: [min] and [max], derived from a [Stream], receive a [Comparator] and return the minimum or maximum element (in this case, the person), rather than the key value. The result is a [Optional<Personne>]: a box containing a person, or an empty box if the stream was empty. [get] returns the contents of the box;
    • lines 31–34: [findFirst] returns the first element of the stream, in a [Optional]; when filtered, the stream returns the first element that satisfies a condition. For the last element of a list, the [getLast] method of the list is sufficient;
    • lines 35–37: There is no one in Brest: [Optional] is empty ([isPresent] returns [false]). Rather than testing it, we transform it: [map(Personne::nom)] transforms its content if there is any; [orElse("personne")] provides the value to use if it is empty;
    • lines 38–43: [orElseThrow] returns the content of [Optional], or throws a [NoSuchElementException] if it is empty. It is used when the absence of a value constitutes an error. [get], used earlier, does the same thing, but its name does not indicate that it can throw an exception; [orElseThrow] is preferred. There is no operation that requires a stream to have exactly one element; you can check the size of the list returned by [toList];
    • line 46: [distinct] removes duplicates (as defined by the [equals] method);
    • lines 49–50: there is no ready-made operation to keep one person per city. Here, we use a set of cities that have already been encountered: [add] returns [true] for a new city (the person is retained) and [false] for a city that has already been encountered. A lambda that modifies an external variable, like this one, should be reserved for streams processed sequentially, which is the default behavior;
    • lines 54–58: [limit(n)] keeps the first n elements, while [skip(n)] skips them. Combined, they extract a “page” of results. [takeWhile] (Java 9) keeps the elements as long as a condition is true and stops at the first element that does not satisfy it; [dropWhile] does the opposite: it skips those elements and keeps all subsequent ones;
    • Line 61: The [gather] (Java 24) operation applies an intermediate collector (“gatherer”) to the stream, which can group, accumulate, or filter elements based on preceding elements. The [Gatherers] class provides several of these; [Gatherers.windowFixed(3)] splits the stream into lists of 3 elements, with the last list potentially being shorter. There are others, such as [windowSliding(n)] (sliding windows), and you can write your own.

    // the API Stream: local records, groupings, joins, collectors
void main() {
    List<Personne> personnes = List.of(
            new Personne("dupont", "jean", 45, "Angers"),
            new Personne("martin", "marie", 17, "Paris"),
            new Personne("durand", "paul", 32, "Angers"),
            new Personne("leroy", "sophie", 28, "Nantes"),
            new Personne("moreau", "luc", 15, "Paris"),
            new Personne("simon", "julie", 52, "Angers"),
            new Personne("laurent", "marc", 32, "Lyon"));
    List<Ville> villes = List.of(
            new Ville("Angers", "Maine-et-Loire"),
            new Ville("Nantes", "Loire-Atlantique"),
            new Ville("Paris", "Paris"),
            new Ville("Brest", "Finistère"));

     // 1 - A local record: a type declared within the method, for an intermediate result
    record Resume(String nom, int decennie) {
    }
    IO.println("[record local]");
    personnes.stream()
            .filter(p -> p.age() > 40)
            .map(p -> new Resume(p.nom(), p.age() / 10 * 10))
            .forEach(r -> IO.println("  " + r.nom() + " a plus de " + r.decennie() + " ans"));

     // 2 - groupingBy: grouping of people by city, in the order of first appearance
    IO.println("[groupingBy]");
    Map<String, List<Personne>> parVille = personnes.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Personne::ville, LinkedHashMap::new, Collectors.toList()));
    parVille.forEach((ville, groupe) -> IO.println("  %s : %d personne(s), âge moyen %.1f (%s)".formatted(
            ville, groupe.size(), groupe.stream().mapToInt(Personne::age).average().orElse(0),
            groupe.stream().map(Personne::nom).collect(Collectors.joining(", ")))));

     // 3 - a join: each person is associated with the city of the same name
    IO.println("[jointure avec flatMap]");
    personnes.stream()
            .flatMap(p -> villes.stream()
                    .filter(v -> v.nom().equals(p.ville()))
                    .map(v -> p.nom() + " habite le département " + v.departement()))
            .forEach(ligne -> IO.println("  " + ligne));
     // the same join using a city dictionary, which is more efficient: a search by person
    Map<String, Ville> villesParNom = villes.stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(Ville::nom, v -> v));
    String jointure = personnes.stream()
            .filter(p -> p.age() >= 18 && villesParNom.containsKey(p.ville()))
            .map(p -> p.nom() + "/" + villesParNom.get(p.ville()).departement())
            .collect(Collectors.joining(", "));
    IO.println("[jointure avec un dictionnaire] " + jointure);

     // 4 - aggregators: toList, toMap, partitioningBy
    List<String> nomsMajeurs = personnes.stream().filter(p -> p.age() >= 18).map(Personne::nom).toList();
    Map<String, Integer> agesParNom = personnes.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.toMap(Personne::nom, Personne::age));
    IO.println("[toList] " + nomsMajeurs.size() + " majeurs ; [toMap] agesParNom.get(\"leroy\")="
            + agesParNom.get("leroy"));
    Map<Boolean, List<String>> majeursMineurs = personnes.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(p -> p.age() >= 18,
                    Collectors.mapping(Personne::nom, Collectors.toList())));
    IO.println("[partitioningBy] majeurs=" + majeursMineurs.get(true)
            + ", mineurs=" + majeursMineurs.get(false));

     // 5 - groupingBy with a downstream collector: count, sum
    Map<String, Long> nombreParVille = personnes.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Personne::ville, TreeMap::new, Collectors.counting()));
    IO.println("[groupingBy + counting] " + nombreParVille);
    Map<String, Integer> sommeParVille = personnes.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Personne::ville, TreeMap::new,
                    Collectors.summingInt(Personne::age)));
    IO.println("[groupingBy + summingInt] " + sommeParVille);

     // 6 - the position of each element in a filtered stream
    IO.println("[position]");
    List<Personne> jeunes = personnes.stream().filter(p -> p.age() < 30).toList();
    IntStream.range(0, jeunes.size()).forEach(i -> IO.println("  " + i + " : " + jeunes.get(i).nom()));
}

record Personne(String nom, String prenom, int age, String ville) {
}

record Ville(String nom, String departement) {
}

    Comments:

    • Lines 18–19: A local record (Java 16), declared within the method where it is used. It allows you to assign a name and a type to the intermediate results of a process without having to declare a class in the program: line 23, each person over 40 is converted into a [Resume] that retains only the relevant data;
    • lines 28–29: The [groupingBy] collector groups elements with the same key—in this case, the city. The result is a dictionary named [Map<String, List<Personne>>]: each city is associated with a list of its residents. Without any other parameters, [groupingBy] creates a [HashMap], in which the order of the keys is unpredictable; here we ask it to create a *[LinkedHashMap]* (***[LinkedHashMap::new]***, manufacturer reference), which keeps the cities in the order of their first appearance. The third parameter is the collector applied to the elements of each group, in this case *[toList]*;
    • lines 30–32: The [forEach] method of a dictionary takes a lambda with two parameters: the key and the value. For each group, it displays its size, average age, and names; the [Collectors.joining(", ")] collector concatenates strings using a separator;
    • lines 36–40: The API stream has no join operation. This is achieved using [flatMap], which replaces each element with a stream and then concatenates all these streams: each person is replaced by the stream of cities with the same name as them (one or none), converted to strings. As in an internal SQL join, only matching pairs are retained: Laurent, who lives in Lyon—which is absent from the list of cities—does not appear, nor does Brest, which has no residents. This code iterates through the entire list of cities for each person;
    • lines 42–47: the same join, but more efficient: the collector [toMap] builds a dictionary of cities, where the key is the city’s name ([Ville::nom]) and the value is the city itself ([v -> v]); we then search this dictionary for the city of each adult. A duplicate key would cause [IllegalStateException] to throw an exception at [toMap];
    • lines 50–54: [toList] and [toMap] perform the processing and store the results in a list and a dictionary, respectively;
    • lines 55–59: [partitioningBy] divides the elements into two groups based on a condition; the result is a dictionary whose keys are [true] and [false]. The collector [mapping(Personne::nom, toList())] converts each person to their name before adding them to their group’s list;
    • lines 62–68: the third parameter of [groupingBy] can be any collector, applied to each group: [counting] counts the elements in the group, [summingInt] adds an integer value ([averagingInt] calculates the average, [maxBy] finds the maximum…). With [TreeMap::new], the cities are sorted;
    • lines 72–73: the position of each element in a filtered stream: the stream is stored in a list, and then the indices are traversed.

    // the API stream: lazy evaluation
void main() {
    List<Integer> nombres = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6));

     // 1 - defining a stream does not execute it
    IO.println("[définition du flux]");
    Stream<Integer> carresPairs = nombres.stream()
            .filter(n -> {
                IO.println("  filter examine " + n);
                return n % 2 == 0;
            })
            .map(n -> {
                IO.println("  map calcule " + n + "*" + n);
                return n * n;
            });
    IO.println("[le flux est défini, rien n'a encore été exécuté]");

     // 2 - It executes during the terminal operation, element by element
    IO.println("[forEach]");
    carresPairs.forEach(c -> IO.println("  forEach reçoit " + c));

     // 3 - A stream is not reusable: to restart the calculation, the stream is recreated
    Supplier<Stream<Integer>> grands = () -> nombres.stream().filter(n -> n > 4);
    IO.println("[avant ajout] grands=" + grands.get().toList());
    nombres.add(10);
    IO.println("[après ajout de 10] grands=" + grands.get().toList());

     // 4 - toList stores the result at a given point in time
    List<Integer> instantane = grands.get().toList();
    nombres.add(20);
    IO.println("[après ajout de 20] grands=" + grands.get().toList() + ", instantane=" + instantane);

     // 5 - findFirst stops the traversal as soon as it finds an element
    IO.println("[findFirst sur un flux]");
    int premier = nombres.stream()
            .filter(n -> {
                IO.println("  filter examine " + n);
                return n > 2;
            })
            .findFirst()
            .orElseThrow();
    IO.println("  premier=" + premier);

     // 6 - `sorted` must know all the elements before passing any of them
    IO.println("[sorted]");
    Stream.of(3, 1, 2)
            .peek(n -> IO.println("  avant sorted : " + n))
            .sorted()
            .forEach(n -> IO.println("  après sorted : " + n));

     // 7 - an int stream: no Integer objects, just calculation methods
    int sommeCarres = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10).filter(n -> n % 2 == 0).map(n -> n * n).sum();
    IO.println("[IntStream] somme des carrés des nombres pairs de 1 à 10 = " + sommeCarres);
    IO.println("[IntStream] boxed : " + IntStream.of(5, 3, 8).boxed().toList()
            + ", asDoubleStream().average() : " + IntStream.of(5, 3, 8).asDoubleStream().average().orElse(0));
}

    Comments:

    • lines 7–15: a stream that keeps even numbers and then calculates their squares. The lambdas here are written with a body enclosed in curly braces, which displays a message before returning its value with [return];
    • Line 3 of the results: After defining the flow, nothing was displayed: neither [filter] nor [map] has yet processed a single element. [carresPairs] does not contain results, but rather a description of a calculation;
    • Lines 4–16 of the results: The calculation runs during the terminal operation [forEach], element by element: each number passes through [filter], then [map] if it is even, and then enters [forEach] before the next number is examined. No intermediate list is constructed;
    • lines 23–26: Since a stream can only be traversed once, we instead store the means to create it: a parameterless lambda [() -> nombres.stream().filter(...)], of type [Supplier<Stream<Integer>>], whose method [get] creates a new stream on each call. The flow created after adding 10 takes this new element into account;
    • lines 29–31: [toList] executes the processing and stores its results: [instantane] is a list that does not see the addition of 20;
    • lines 35–42: [findFirst] stops iterating as soon as it finds an element: the numbers following 3 are never examined. [anyMatch], [limit], [takeWhile]… likewise stop the iteration as early as possible; this is what allows infinite streams to be processed;
    • Lines 46–49: Some intermediate operations cannot process elements one by one: [sorted] must know all the elements in order to transmit the smallest one. The operation [peek], which executes a lambda on each element as it passes through without modifying it, shows that the three elements are received by [sorted] before it transmits a single one;
    • lines 52–55: the primitive streams [IntStream], [LongStream], and [DoubleStream] prevent the creation of objects [Integer], [Long], and [Double]. [IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10)] generates the integers from 1 to 10 (including 10). [boxed] converts a [IntStream] to [Stream<Integer>], and a [asDoubleStream] to [DoubleStream]. A [double] concatenated with a string is displayed with all its decimal places and a decimal point; to limit the number of decimal places, you would use [formatted].

    Lazy evaluation has two practical consequences:

    • a stream can only be traversed once. If the result of a calculation is needed multiple times, it is stored in a list using [toList];
    • operations can be chained together at no cost: chaining [filter], [map], and [limit] creates no intermediate collection, and only the necessary elements are computed.

    Finally, note that the [parallelStream] method of a collection returns a stream whose elements are processed simultaneously by multiple threads (Chapter 8). It only speeds up time-consuming operations on large volumes of data and requires lambdas with no side effects: it should only be used after assessing its benefits. We will encounter the API stream throughout the course, and in Chapter 7 we will see how the functional interfaces it uses are constructed.

    5.6. Text files

    Java has two API packages for files: the [java.io] package, which has been available since Java 1.0 ([File], [FileReader], [FileInputStream]…), and the [java.nio.file] package, introduced with Java 7 ([Path], [Files]…). The latter is more comprehensive and provides better error reporting: it is the one you should use today. It relies on the read and write classes of [java.io] ([BufferedReader], [BufferedWriter]…), which are obtained through methods of the [Files] class.

    A file is represented by a [java.nio.file.Path] object, created by [Path.of("infos.txt")] (Java 11). A relative path, such as this one, is supplemented by the program’s current directory—the one from which it was launched.

    Since Java 18 (JEP 400), the default encoding for text files is UTF-8, regardless of the operating system. Previously, it depended on the system (often Windows-1252 on French-language Windows), and the same program could interpret the same file differently depending on the machine. The methods of the [Files] class had already been using UTF-8 by default since Java 8.

    5.6.1. The BufferedReader class

    The [java.io.BufferedReader] class allows you to read the contents of a text file line by line. It is actually capable of processing streams that are not files (a network connection, for example). It reads the file in blocks, which it stores in a buffer: most reading is done in memory, without accessing the disk.

    Method
    role
    [static BufferedReader Files.newBufferedReader(Path path)]
    opens the file [path] for reading as UTF-8; an overload allows you to specify the encoding: [Files.newBufferedReader(path, StandardCharsets.ISO_8859_1)]
    [String readLine()]
    returns the next line of the stream, without the end-of-line marker, or [null] if at the end of the stream
    [int read()]
    returns the next character in the stream, or -1 at the end of the stream
    [Stream<String> lines()]
    returns the remaining lines as a stream from the API stream
    [void close()]
    closes the stream and releases the resources allocated for its management. This must be done after processing the stream, which is handled by the [try] instruction with resources

    // reading a text file with BufferedReader
void main(String[] args) {
     // the current directory: this is where files specified by a relative path are searched for
    IO.println("Dossier courant : " + Path.of("").toAbsolutePath().getFileName());
     // The file name can be passed as an argument; otherwise, infos.txt
    Path fichier = Path.of(args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "infos.txt");
    try {
         // Read mode 1: line by line
        IO.println("Lecture 1----------------");
        try (BufferedReader lecteur = Files.newBufferedReader(fichier)) {
            String ligne;
             // readLine sets the value to null at the end of the file
            while ((ligne = lecteur.readLine()) != null) {
                IO.println(ligne);
            }
        } // Here, the stream is closed

         // Read 2: the entire file at once
        IO.println("Lecture 2----------------");
        IO.print(Files.readString(fichier));
    } catch (NoSuchFileException e) {
         // e.getFile() is the path to the file that cannot be found
        IO.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : le fichier [" + e.getFile() + "] n'existe pas");
    } catch (IOException e) {
         // other I/O errors
        IO.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
    }
}

    Comments:

    • line 2: the [main] method receives the command-line arguments here, in the [args] array;
    • Line 4: Displays the name of the current folder, the one from which the [java] command was launched. [Path.of("")] refers to the current folder; [toAbsolutePath] converts it to a full path, of which [getFileName] retains only the last element, so as not to clutter the results with a full path;
    • line 6: The file being read is [infos.txt] or the one passed as an argument. Since this is a relative path, it is searched for in the current directory;
    • line 10: The [try (déclaration de ressource) { ... }] statement, known as a “try-with-resources” block (Java 7), ensures that the stream is closed upon exiting the block, even if an exception occurs within the block. It eliminates the need to explicitly call the [close] method. It applies to any object that implements the [AutoCloseable] interface—that is, any object with a [close] method that releases resources (file, network connection, database connection, etc.). Prior to Java 7, the stream had to be closed in a [finally] clause after verifying that it had indeed been opened;
    • lines 13–15: the file is read line by line. The assignment [ligne = lecteur.readLine()] is an expression whose value is that of [ligne]: it is compared to [null], which indicates the end of the file;
    • Line 20: [Files.readString] (Java 11) reads the entire file at once and closes it;
    • Lines 21–27: Input/output errors are signaled by exceptions derived from [java.io.IOException]. These are controlled exceptions (Chapter 4): the compiler requires that they be caught or declared. A missing file triggers a [NoSuchFileException], which is derived from it; therefore, it must be caught first. Its method [getFile] returns the path of the file being searched for. The older classes of [java.io] report the same error as a [FileNotFoundException].

IOException : Is a directory

    Choosing the current directory to locate data files is natural for a compact source file that is run from its own directory. For a Maven project, the command [mvn exec:java] runs in the project directory: that is where we will place the data files for the example application.

    5.6.2. The BufferedWriter class

    The [java.io.BufferedWriter] class allows you to write to a text file. Like [BufferedReader], it uses a buffer and is capable of handling streams that are not files.

    Method
    Role
    [static BufferedWriter Files.newBufferedWriter(Path path)]
    Opens the file [path] for writing as UTF-8. The file is created, or cleared if it already exists. Optional parameters allow you to specify the encoding and the opening mode: [Files.newBufferedWriter(path, StandardOpenOption.APPEND)] appends the writes to the end of the existing file
    [void write(String str)]
    writes [str] to the file
    [void newLine()]
    writes a line-end character: the system’s default, “\r\n” on Windows, “\n” on Linux, and macOS
    [void flush()]
    writes the contents of the buffer to the file without waiting for it to be full
    [void close()]
    closes the stream after writing the buffer’s contents to the file. This must be done after processing the stream

    Writes to a [BufferedWriter] are not immediate: the text is first written to the buffer, then to the file when the buffer is full, when it is explicitly flushed using the [flush] method, or when the stream is closed. This is the most efficient mode for files because it minimizes disk access. It is not suitable for all data streams, particularly network streams: in a dialogue between two partners, what one writes must be read immediately by the other, and the buffer must be flushed after each message. The [java.io.PrintWriter] class, which we will use later, adds the methods [print], [println], and [printf], and can automatically clear its buffer after each call to [println] (constructor [new PrintWriter(writer, true)]).

    // Writing a text file with BufferedWriter
void main() {
    Path fichier = Path.of("infos2.txt");
    try {
         // creating the text file (if it already exists, it is overwritten)
        try (BufferedWriter ecrivain = Files.newBufferedWriter(fichier)) {
            IO.println("encodage par défaut : " + Charset.defaultCharset());
             // Loop as long as the entered line is not empty
            while (true) {
                String saisie = IO.readln("ligne (rien pour arrêter) : ");
                String ligne = saisie == null ? "" : saisie.strip();
                if (ligne.isEmpty()) {
                    break;
                }
                 // Write the line to the text file, followed by a newline
                ecrivain.write(ligne);
                ecrivain.newLine();
            }
        } // close the stream: the buffer is written to the file

         // Verification: Reads the created file
        IO.println("Contenu de " + fichier + " (" + Files.size(fichier) + " octets) :");
        IO.print(Files.readString(fichier));
    } catch (IOException e) {
        IO.println("L'erreur suivante s'est produite : " + e);
    }
}

    Comments:

    • line 6: once again, we use the [try] statement with resources so that we don’t have to explicitly close the stream. This closure occurs automatically at the end of the block (closing curly brace on line 19). It is this closure that writes the text remaining in the buffer to the file; without it, the file might remain incomplete;
    • line 7: the default encoding, UTF-8;
    • lines 16–17: writes a line to the text file, followed by a line break;
    • line 22: the [Files.size] method returns the size of a file in bytes. The 25 bytes break down as follows: 21 characters, plus 1 additional byte for each of the two [è] (which take up 2 bytes in UTF-8), plus two one-byte line breaks ("\n" on Linux, where the tests were run; on Windows, each "\r\n" line break would take up 2 bytes);
    • Line 24: Why [try / catch]? We could use a filename in the form [rep1/rep2/fichier] with a folder named [rep1/rep2] that does not exist, making it impossible to create the file. A [NoSuchFileException] exception, derived from [IOException], would then be thrown. There are other possible exception scenarios (disk full, insufficient permissions, etc.). In any case, the compiler requires that the controlled exceptions [IOException] thrown by [newBufferedWriter], [write], or [size] be handled.

    5.6.3. The Files and Path Classes

    For common operations, the utility class [Files] eliminates the need to handle streams: a single method opens the file, reads or writes it in its entirety, and then closes it. It also allows you to create, copy, move, and delete files and folders. The [Path] interface handles paths.

    Method
    role
    [Files.readString(path)]
    returns the file’s contents as a string (Java 11)
    [Files.readAllLines(path)]
    returns the lines of the file in a list [List<String>]
    [Files.lines(path)]
    Returns the lines of the file as a stream ([Stream<String>]) that is read on demand and must be closed after use
    [Files.writeString(path, texte, options...)]
    creates (or overwrites) the file and writes [texte] (Java 11) to it; with the [StandardOpenOption.APPEND] option, appends the text to the end of the file
    [Files.write(path, lignes, options...)]
    writes a collection of lines, each followed by a newline
    [Files.readAllBytes(path)], [Files.write(path, octets)]
    reads and writes the file as a byte array
    [Files.exists(path)], [Files.size(path)], [Files.delete(path)], [Files.copy(source, cible)], [Files.move(source, cible)]
    checks if a file exists, returns its size, deletes it, copies it, moves it
    [Files.createDirectories(path)]
    creates the folder and its parent folders if they do not exist
    [Files.list(dossier)], [Files.walk(dossier)]
    the elements of the folder and its entire tree structure, in the form of a stream [Stream<Path>]
    [path.resolve(autre)]
    builds a path by appending [autre] to [path], using the system separator
    [path.getFileName()], [path.getParent()], [path.toAbsolutePath()]
    the file name, its folder, and its full path

    // The Path and Files classes
void main() throws IOException {
     // resolve constructs a path using the system separator (\ on Windows, / on Linux)
    Path dossier = Path.of("donnees");
    Path chemin = dossier.resolve("villes.txt");
    String nom = chemin.getFileName().toString();
    IO.println("chemin=" + chemin + ", nom=" + nom + ", dossier=" + chemin.getParent()
            + ", sans extension=" + nom.substring(0, nom.lastIndexOf('.')));

     // createDirectories creates the folder (and its parent folders) if it does not exist
    Files.createDirectories(dossier);

     // writeString: creates (or overwrites) a file with the given text, in UTF-8
    Files.writeString(chemin, "Angers\nNantes\n");
     // write with the option APPEND: adds lines to the end of the file
    Files.write(chemin, List.of("Paris", "Lyon"), StandardOpenOption.APPEND);
     // readAllLines: all lines in a list
    List<String> lignes = Files.readAllLines(chemin);
    IO.println("readAllLines : " + lignes.size() + " lignes " + lignes);
     // readString: the entire file in a string
    IO.println("readString : " + Files.readString(chemin).length() + " caractères");
     // lines: a stream of lines read on demand; close after use
    try (Stream<String> flux = Files.lines(chemin)) {
        flux.filter(l -> l.startsWith("N") || l.startsWith("L"))
                .forEach(ville -> IO.println("lines + filter : " + ville));
    }

     // encoding: UTF-8 by default; another encoding can be specified
    String texte = "élève";
    Files.writeString(dossier.resolve("utf8.txt"), texte);
    Files.writeString(dossier.resolve("utf8bom.txt"), "\uFEFF" + texte);
    Files.writeString(dossier.resolve("latin1.txt"), texte, StandardCharsets.ISO_8859_1);
    HexFormat hex = HexFormat.of().withUpperCase();
    for (String fichier : List.of("utf8.txt", "utf8bom.txt", "latin1.txt")) {
        byte[] octets = Files.readAllBytes(dossier.resolve(fichier));
        IO.println("%-12s: %2d octets : %s".formatted(fichier, octets.length, hex.formatHex(octets)));
    }
     // a Latin-1 file re-read in UTF-8: readString rejects invalid bytes
    Path latin1 = dossier.resolve("latin1.txt");
    try {
        IO.println(Files.readString(latin1));
    } catch (MalformedInputException e) {
        IO.println("latin1.txt lu en UTF-8 : " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
    }
     // new String(bytes, UTF_8) replaces each invalid byte with the character �
    IO.println("latin1.txt décodé en UTF-8 : "
            + new String(Files.readAllBytes(latin1), StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
    IO.println("latin1.txt lu en Latin-1 : " + Files.readString(latin1, StandardCharsets.ISO_8859_1));
     // the BOM is not removed during reading: it is an extra character
    IO.println("utf8bom.txt : " + Files.readString(dossier.resolve("utf8bom.txt")).length() + " caractères");

     // exists, list
    IO.println("exists(villes.txt)=" + Files.exists(chemin) + ", exists(xx.txt)="
            + Files.exists(dossier.resolve("xx.txt")));
    try (Stream<Path> fichiers = Files.list(dossier)) {
        for (Path fichier : fichiers.sorted().toList()) {
            IO.println("  %-12s %3d octets".formatted(fichier.getFileName(), Files.size(fichier)));
        }
    }

     // cleanup: a folder must be empty to be deleted; its contents are deleted first
    try (Stream<Path> arbre = Files.walk(dossier)) {
        for (Path p : arbre.sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder()).toList()) {
            Files.delete(p);
        }
    }
    IO.println("après suppression : exists(donnees)=" + Files.exists(dossier));
}

    Comments:

    • Line 2: The methods in [Files] call [IOException]. To keep this demo program lightweight, the [main] method declares them using the [throws IOException] clause instead of intercepting them: an error would terminate the program and display the exception;
    • Lines 4–8: [resolve] uses the system’s path separator. The course runs were performed on Linux: the resulting path is [donnees/villes.txt]; on Windows, it would be [donnees\villes.txt]. Building paths using [resolve] (or [Path.of("donnees", "villes.txt")]) rather than concatenating strings makes the code portable. Since [Path] does not have a method that returns a file extension, it is separated from the name using [lastIndexOf];
    • Line 11: Creating the folder [donnees] does not cause an error if it already exists;
    • Lines 14–21: writing, adding, and reading, each in a single statement;
    • Lines 23–26: [Files.lines] returns a stream: the lines are read one by one as the program processes them. You can apply the API stream to it, and thus process a file several gigabytes in size without loading it into memory, which is what [readAllLines] would do. The stream keeps the file open: it must be closed, hence the [try] instruction with resources ([Stream] implements [AutoCloseable]);
    • lines 29–37: the same text “élève” is written using three encodings, then the bytes in the files are displayed in hexadecimal using the [HexFormat] class (Java 17):
      • In UTF-8, Java’s default encoding, accented characters take up 2 bytes (é = C3 A9) and the others 1 byte: 7 bytes for 5 characters;
      • in UTF-8 with BOM (Byte Order Mark), the file begins with the 3 bytes EF BB BF, which signal to software that the file is encoded in UTF-8. Java never writes BOM on its own: it is obtained by writing the character U+FEFF at the beginning of the text, denoted as ["\uFEFF"];
      • in Latin-1 (ISO-8859-1), the traditional encoding for Western European texts, each character occupies one byte (é = E9);
    • Lines 39–44: Reading a file using an encoding different from the one used to write it alters accented characters: the byte sequence E9 6C E8 is invalid in UTF-8. [Files.readString] and [Files.readAllLines] reject such a file by throwing a [MalformedInputException] exception (derived from [IOException]);
    • Lines 46–47: The conversion of a byte array to a string by the [new String(octets, encodage)] constructor is less strict: each invalid byte is replaced by the character �. A [InputStreamReader] behaves the same way; in contrast, the [BufferedReader] returned by [Files.newBufferedReader] is strict, like [Files.readString], and also calls a [MalformedInputException];
    • line 48: when read with the correct encoding, the file is correct;
    • line 50: Upon reading, Java does not recognize the BOM: it is read as an invisible character at the beginning of the text, which has 6 characters instead of 5. If you need to read UTF-8 files generated with a BOM (by certain Windows software), you must remove this character yourself. Today, the rule is simple: write and read text files in UTF-8, without BOM;
    • lines 53–59: the files in the folder. [Files.list] returns a stream that must be closed, just like the one for [Files.lines], and does not guarantee the order of the names: [sorted] sorts them;
    • lines 62–67: deleting the folder. [Files.delete] refuses to delete a non-empty folder: we traverse the entire directory tree using [Files.walk], and sort the paths in reverse order ([Comparator.reverseOrder()]) to delete a folder’s contents before the folder itself.

    The methods of [Files] block the thread that calls them until the operation is complete. In Chapter 9, which covers asynchronous programming, we’ll see how to avoid blocking a program during a long I/O operation.

    5.7. Binary Files

    5.7.1. The DataOutputStream and DataInputStream classes

    The classes [java.io.DataOutputStream] and [java.io.DataInputStream] are used to write to and read from binary files. In such a file, data is not written as text but in its internal form: a [int] always occupies 4 bytes, regardless of its value. These are byte streams: they are derived from the classes [OutputStream] and [InputStream], whereas text streams are derived from [Writer] and [Reader].

    // syntax: java Fichiers04.java binary text logs
// Reads a text file (text) and stores its contents in a binary file (binary)
// The text file contains lines in the form "name: age," which are written as (String, int)
// (logs) is a text file containing logs
void main(String[] args) {
     // Three arguments are required
    if (args.length != 3) {
        IO.println("syntaxe : java Fichiers04.java texte binaire logs");
        System.exit(1);
    }
     // Opening the three files; they will be closed at the end of the `try` block, in reverse order
    try (BufferedReader input = Files.newBufferedReader(Path.of(args[0]));
         DataOutputStream output = new DataOutputStream(
                 new BufferedOutputStream(Files.newOutputStream(Path.of(args[1]))));
         PrintWriter logs = new PrintWriter(Files.newBufferedWriter(Path.of(args[2])))) {
         // Processing the text file
        String ligne;
        int numLigne = 0, nbPersonnes = 0;
        while ((ligne = input.readLine()) != null) {
             // one more line
            numLigne++;
             // Empty line? Ignore it
            if (ligne.isBlank()) {
                continue;
            }
             // a line containing name: age
            String[] champs = ligne.strip().split("\\s*:\\s*");
             // We need 2 fields
            if (champs.length != 2) {
                logs.println("La ligne n° [" + numLigne + "] du fichier [" + args[0]
                        + "] a un nombre de champs incorrect");
                continue;
            }
             // The first field must not be empty
            boolean erreur = false;
            String nom = champs[0];
            if (nom.isEmpty()) {
                logs.println("La ligne n° [" + numLigne + "] du fichier [" + args[0] + "] a un nom vide");
                erreur = true;
            }
             // The second field must be an integer >= 0
            int age = entier(champs[1]);
            if (age < 0) {
                logs.println("La ligne n° [" + numLigne + "] du fichier [" + args[0] + "] a un âge ["
                        + champs[1] + "] incorrect");
                erreur = true;
            }
             // If there are no errors, write the data to the binary file
            if (!erreur) {
                output.writeUTF(nom);
                output.writeInt(age);
                nbPersonnes++;
            }
        }
        IO.println(numLigne + " lignes lues, " + nbPersonnes + " personnes écrites dans [" + args[1]
                + "], erreurs dans [" + args[2] + "]");
    } catch (NoSuchFileException e) {
        IO.println("Le fichier [" + e.getFile() + "] n'existe pas");
        System.exit(2);
    } catch (IOException e) {
        IO.println("L'erreur suivante s'est produite : " + e);
        System.exit(3);
    }
}

// a positive integer or zero; -1 if the string is not an integer
int entier(String champ) {
    try {
        return Integer.parseInt(champ);
    } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
        return -1;
    }
}

    Let’s take a closer look at the operations related to class [DataOutputStream]:

    • Lines 13–14: The [DataOutputStream] object is built around another byte stream, following the principle of nested streams (the “decorator” design pattern):
      • [Files.newOutputStream(Path.of(args[1]))] writes a byte stream to the file, which is created or flushed if it already exists;
      • [BufferedOutputStream] adds a buffer to it, so as not to access the disk with every write;
      • [DataOutputStream] adds methods for writing basic data types;
    • Lines 50–51: the write operations. The [DataOutputStream] class has one method per simple data type: [writeInt], [writeDouble], [writeLong], [writeBoolean], [writeUTF] for a string…;
    • Lines 12–15: The three streams are opened in a single [try] statement with resources, with their declarations separated by semicolons. They will be closed at the end of the [try] block, in the reverse order in which they were opened. Closing the outer stream ([DataOutputStream]) closes the streams it contains. The log file is written via a [PrintWriter], to make use of the [println] method;
    • line 27: the separator is the character [:], surrounded by any spaces, which are removed along with it;
    • Lines 42–47: The age must be a positive integer or zero. Java does not have a method that converts a string to an integer without throwing an exception in case of an error: the method [entier] (lines 67–73) catches the exception [NumberFormatException] and returns -1, which is an invalid value for an age;
    • lines 9, 59, 62: [System.exit(n)] terminates the program with exit code n, which a script can check (0: success; this is the exit code of a program whose [main] method terminates normally).

    The contents of the binary file [personnes1.bin] can be displayed in hexadecimal using the Linux command [od] (on Windows, the command PowerShell [Format-Hex] produces a similar display):

    1
2

    > od -A d -t x1z personnes1.bin
0000000 00 04 70 61 75 6c 00 00 00 0a 00 06 68 65 6c 65  >..paul......hele<
0000016 6e 65 00 00 00 0f 00 07 6a 61 63 71 75 65 73 00  >ne......jacques.<
0000032 00 00 0b 00 07 73 79 6c 76 61 69 6e 00 00 00 0c  >.....sylvain....<
0000048

    This shows how [DataOutputStream] writes the data:

    • a string is written by [writeUTF], preceded by its length in bytes, on 2 bytes: 00 04, followed by the 4 bytes of “paul” (70 61 75 6c). The characters are encoded using a variant of UTF-8;
    • an integer [int] is written over 4 bytes, with the most significant byte first (known as “big-endian” order, used in network protocols): 10 is written as 00 00 00 0a. This format is the same on all machines: a file written by [DataOutputStream] on Windows can be read on Linux;
    • the data is written consecutively, without any separators or line breaks: the file is 48 bytes long (line 5: with the [-A d] option, [od] displays the positions in decimal).

    To read this file, you must therefore know the exact order and type of the written data. For each method [writeXX] of [DataOutputStream], the class [DataInputStream] has a corresponding method [readXX]: [readUTF], [readInt], [readDouble]… However, it cannot indicate how many bytes remain to be read: a file read by [DataInputStream] must begin with the number of records it contains, or be read until the [EOFException] exception occurs, which signals the end of the stream. However, an exception must remain exceptional, and the end of a file is not.

    5.7.2. The RandomAccessFile class

    The [java.io.RandomAccessFile] class reads from and writes to a file using direct access: you can position the read/write head at any location in the file before reading or writing. It has the same read and write methods as [DataInputStream] and [DataOutputStream] (it implements the same interfaces, [DataInput] and [DataOutput]), and additionally:

    method
    role
    [RandomAccessFile(String name, String mode)]
    opens the file for reading ([mode] "r") or for reading and writing ("rw")
    [long length()]
    the file size, in bytes
    [long getFilePointer()]
    the current position in the file
    [void seek(long pos)]
    moves to position [pos] in the file

    The program [Fichiers05.java] performs the reverse operation of the previous program: it reads the binary file to create a text file. If the resulting text file contains the correct data from the original file, we will know that the text → binary → text conversion was successful.

    // syntax: java Fichiers05.java binary text
// Reads a binary file (binary) and stores its contents in a text file (text)
// the binary file contains (String, int) pairs
// The text file will contain lines in the form name:age
void main(String[] args) {
     // Two arguments are required
    if (args.length != 2) {
        IO.println("syntaxe : java Fichiers05.java binaire texte");
        System.exit(1);
    }
     // Open the binary file for reading ("r") and the text file for writing
    try (RandomAccessFile input = new RandomAccessFile(args[0], "r");
         PrintWriter output = new PrintWriter(Files.newBufferedWriter(Path.of(args[1])))) {
         // Process the binary file until the end of the file is reached
        int nbPersonnes = 0;
        while (input.getFilePointer() < input.length()) {
             // Read "name," then "age": in the order they were written
            String nom = input.readUTF();
            int age = input.readInt();
             // Write to the text file
            output.println(nom + ":" + age);
            nbPersonnes++;
        }
        IO.println(nbPersonnes + " personnes lues dans [" + args[0] + "] et écrites dans [" + args[1] + "]");
         // direct access: return to the beginning of the file and reread the first person
        input.seek(0);
        IO.println("première personne : " + input.readUTF() + ", " + input.readInt() + " ans");
    } catch (EOFException e) {
         // the file ends in the middle of a record
        IO.println("Le fichier [" + args[0] + "] est tronqué");
        System.exit(2);
    } catch (FileNotFoundException e) {
         // RandomAccessFile indicates a missing file with a FileNotFoundException
        IO.println(e.getMessage());
        System.exit(3);
    } catch (IOException e) {
        IO.println("L'erreur suivante s'est produite : " + e);
        System.exit(4);
    }
}

    Let’s take a closer look at the operations involving the [RandomAccessFile] class:

    • line 12: the [RandomAccessFile] object is opened in read-only mode (“r” mode);
    • lines 18–19: the read operations, [readUTF] and [readInt]. They must be called in the order of the writes;
    • line 16: reading continues until the current position in the file reaches the end of the file;
    • lines 26–27: direct access: [seek] resets the position to the beginning of the file, and the first record is read again. If all records were the same size, we could read the nth record directly by moving to position n × size: this is the principle behind direct-access files, the precursors to databases;
    • line 28: the exception [EOFException] now signals a true anomaly: a file that ends in the middle of a record;
    • line 32: [RandomAccessFile], a subclass of [java.io], signals a missing file via a [FileNotFoundException], whose message—provided by the system—contains the file name.

    Java also has a mechanism for binary serialization of objects: the classes *[ObjectOutputStream] and [ObjectInputStream] write and read entire objects, provided that their class implements the *[java.io.Serializable] interface. This mechanism is now deprecated: deserializing data from an untrusted source has enabled numerous attacks, as deserialization can execute code chosen by the attacker. A text-based format such as JSON is preferred instead. However, the [Serializable] interface is still found in many classes, particularly exceptions, which inherit it from the [Throwable] class: which is why the compiler, when using the [-Xlint:all] option, requires that they declare a [serialVersionUID] field, as we will see in the sample application.

    5.7.3. JSON Serialization with Jackson

    Writing to and reading from a binary file one data point at a time is tedious, and even the slightest discrepancy between writing and reading produces incorrect results. It is generally preferable to serialize objects: automatically converting them into a sequence of characters, then deserializing them to reconstruct them.

    JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text-based, human-readable, and universal format: it is the exchange format for web services (Chapter 13) and many configuration files. An object is written within curly braces as pairs of "property": value, or as an array enclosed in square brackets.

    The Java standard library cannot read or write JSON. An external library is used; the most common one is Jackson, which Spring Boot uses by default. Version 3 (2025) has changed packages: [tools.jackson.*] instead of [com.fasterxml.jackson.*] for version 2, which is still commonly encountered; its annotations remain in the [com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation] package. An external library is obtained using Maven (Chapter 2): the program is therefore a Maven project, [Fichiers06], with the following directory structure:

    package json;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonProperty;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;
import tools.jackson.core.JacksonException;
import tools.jackson.core.json.JsonWriteFeature;
import tools.jackson.core.type.TypeReference;
import tools.jackson.databind.MapperFeature;
import tools.jackson.databind.SerializationFeature;
import tools.jackson.databind.json.JsonMapper;

// Serialization JSON with Jackson 3
public class Fichiers06 {

     // a person: a record, whose components become properties JSON
    record Personne(String nom, int age, List<String> loisirs) {
    }

     // an article: the @JsonProperty annotation sets the property name JSON
    record Article(@JsonProperty("reference") String code, BigDecimal prix) {
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        List<Personne> personnes = List.of(
                new Personne("paul", 10, List.of("football")),
                new Personne("hélène", 15, List.of("piano", "tennis")),
                new Personne("jacques", 11, List.of()));

         // 1 - a JsonMapper with the default configuration: a single line
        JsonMapper mapper = JsonMapper.builder().build();
        String json = mapper.writeValueAsString(personnes.get(1));
        IO.println("[par défaut] " + json);
         // Non-ASCII characters can be escaped
        JsonMapper ascii = JsonMapper.builder().enable(JsonWriteFeature.ESCAPE_NON_ASCII).build();
        IO.println("[ESCAPE_NON_ASCII] " + ascii.writeValueAsString(personnes.get(1)));

         // 2 - an option: indentation
        JsonMapper indente = JsonMapper.builder().enable(SerializationFeature.INDENT_OUTPUT).build();
        json = indente.writeValueAsString(personnes);
         // writing to a text file
        Path fichier = Path.of("personnes.json");
        Files.writeString(fichier, json);
        IO.println("[personnes.json]");
        IO.println(Files.readString(fichier));

         // 3 - deserialization: from JSON text to objects
        String texte = Files.readString(fichier);
         // TypeReference passes the full type `List<Person>` to Jackson
        List<Personne> relues = mapper.readValue(texte, new TypeReference<List<Personne>>() {
        });
        IO.println("[relues] " + relues.size() + " personnes");
        for (Personne p : relues) {
            IO.println("  " + p.nom() + ", " + p.age() + " ans, loisirs : " + p.loisirs());
        }

         // 4 - a property name specified by an annotation
        String jsonArticle = mapper.writeValueAsString(new Article("A12", new BigDecimal("12.5")));
        IO.println("[@JsonProperty] " + jsonArticle);
         // Parsing can ignore case in property names
        JsonMapper casse = JsonMapper.builder()
                .enable(MapperFeature.ACCEPT_CASE_INSENSITIVE_PROPERTIES)
                .build();
        Article article = casse.readValue("""
                { "REFERENCE": "B7", "Prix": 3 }""", Article.class);
        IO.println("[ACCEPT_CASE_INSENSITIVE_PROPERTIES] " + article);

         // 5 - an invalid JSON document causes a JacksonException
        try {
            mapper.readValue("""
                    { "nom": "x", "age": "douze" }""", Personne.class);
        } catch (JacksonException e) {
            IO.println("[erreur] " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getOriginalMessage());
            IO.println("[erreur] ligne " + e.getLocation().getLineNr() + ", colonne "
                    + e.getLocation().getColumnNr() + ", chemin : " + e.getPathReference());
        }
    }
}
