    Comments:

    • line 1: In a Maven project, classes are organized into packages: the class [Fichiers06] from the package [json] is located in the file [src/main/java/json/Fichiers06.java];
    • Lines 3–14: Unlike a compact source file, a regular class must import the classes it uses, including those from the standard library;
    • lines 20–21: the [Personne] record to be serialized, declared in the [Fichiers06] class. Jackson 3 can serialize a record: each component becomes a JSON property with the same name;
    • lines 24–25: the annotation [@JsonProperty] sets the name of a component’s JSON property to [reference] instead of [code];
    • line 27: the method [main] is a static method of a class. It declares the exception [IOException], which can be thrown by methods of [Files];
    • lines 34–36: A [JsonMapper] is created by an object builder: [JsonMapper.builder()] returns an object to which the desired options are specified, and then [build] creates the [JsonMapper]. With the default options, the text is written on a single line, and accented characters are written as-is (line 2 of the results);
    • Lines 38–39: The [ESCAPE_NON_ASCII] option instructs the system to write non-ASCII characters as escape sequences: [é] becomes [\u00E9]. The text remains correct, but it is difficult to read; this is useful when the text JSON must pass through a system that only recognizes ASCII;
    • lines 42–43: The option [INDENT_OUTPUT] produces indented text spread across multiple lines. A list is serialized into an array JSON;
    • lines 45–48: the text JSON is written to a text file and then read back to be displayed: this is how binary serialization is replaced today;
    • lines 53–54: deserialization reconstructs the list. Jackson creates the objects [Personne] by calling the record’s constructor, whose parameters are associated with the JSON properties of the same name. For a list, you must specify the type of its elements to Jackson. However, the expression [List<Personne>.class] does not exist: Java generics are erased at compile time (“type erasure”), and at runtime there is only a [List] class, without any type parameters. The trick with [TypeReference] is to create an anonymous class ([new TypeReference<List<Personne>>() { }]***) derived from [TypeReference<List<Personne>>]***: the parent type of a class is preserved in the compiled code, and Jackson can read it. For an array, which is simpler, we write [Personne[].class];
    • lines 61–62: serialization of a [Article]: the property [reference] has the name specified by the annotation. A [BigDecimal] is written as a number JSON;
    • lines 64–69: With the [ACCEPT_CASE_INSENSITIVE_PROPERTIES] option, Jackson ignores case in property names during parsing: [REFERENCE] and [Prix] are accepted;
    • lines 72–79: An invalid JSON document—in this case, a string where a number is expected—triggers an exception derived from [JacksonException], in this case [InvalidFormatException]. In Jackson 3, these exceptions are unchecked (they are derived from [RuntimeException]), whereas in Jackson 2 they were derived from [IOException]. [getOriginalMessage] returns the message without the location information, which [getLocation] and [getPathReference] provide separately: row 1, column 22, property [age] of record [Personne].

    A [JsonMapper] is costly to create, but once created, it is reusable and can be shared among multiple threads: a program typically creates only one, stored in a constant. We will use JSON in the following example application and throughout the course.

    5.8. Regular Expressions

    The [java.util.regex] package supports the use of regular expressions. These allow you to validate the format of a string. For example, you can verify that a string representing a date is indeed in the dd/mm/yy format. To do this, you use a pattern and compare the string to that pattern. In this example, d, m, and y must be digits. The pattern for a valid date format is therefore [\d\d/\d\d/\d\d], where the symbol [\d] represents a digit. The symbols that can be used in a pattern are as follows:

    character
    description
    [\]
    marks the following character as a special character or literal. For example, [n] corresponds to the character n, [\n] corresponds to a newline character, [\\] corresponds to \, and [\(] corresponds to (
    [^]
    corresponds to the beginning of the string
    [$]
    corresponds to the end of the string
    [*]
    matches the preceding element zero or more times. Thus, [zo*] matches z or zoo
    [+]
    matches the preceding element one or more times. Thus, [zo+] matches "zoo," but not "z"
    [?]
    matches the preceding element zero or one time. For example, [a?ve?] matches "ve" in "lever"
    [.]
    matches any single character, except for a newline character
    [(modèle)]
    searches for the pattern and stores the match (a group). The matching substring can be extracted from the result using the [group] method. To find matches with characters in parentheses, use [\(] or [\)]
    [x|y]
    matches either x or y. For example, [z|foot] matches z or foot; [(z|f)oo] matches zoo or foo
    [{n}]
    n is a non-negative integer. Corresponds exactly n times to the previous element. For example, [o{2}] does not correspond to o in Bob, but to the first two o’s in fooooot
    [{n,}]
    matches the previous element at least n times. For example, [o{2,}] does not match the 'o' in "Bob," but matches all the 'o's in "fooooot." [o{1,}] is equivalent to [o+], and [o{0,}] is equivalent to [o*]
    [{n,m}]
    matches the previous element at least n times and at most m times. For example, [o{1,3}] matches the first three “o”s in “foooooot”; [o{0,1}] is equivalent to [o?]
    [[xyz]]
    character set: matches one of the specified characters. For example, [[abc]] matches the letter “a” in “plat”
    [[^xyz]]
    negative character set: matches any character not listed. For example, [[^abc]] matches "p" in "plat"
    [[a-z]]
    Character range: matches any character in the specified range, in this case a lowercase unaccented letter
    [[^m-z]]
    negative character range: matches any character not between 'm' and 'z'
    [\b]
    matches a word boundary, that is, the position between a word character and a non-word character. For example, [er\b] matches "er" in "lever," but not "er" in "verb"
    [\B]
    corresponds to a position that is not a word boundary. [en*t\B] corresponds to “ent” in “bien entendu”
    [\d]
    matches a digit; is equivalent to [[0-9]]
    [\D]
    corresponds to a character that is not a digit
    [\f], [\n], [\r], [\t]
    correspond to the characters page break, new line, carriage return, and tab, respectively
    [\s]
    corresponds to any whitespace: space, tab, page break, line break… Equivalent to [[ \t\n\x0B\f\r]]
    [\S]
    matches any character that is not a whitespace character
    [\w]
    matches any word character: by default in Java, this is an unaccented letter, a digit, or an underscore; equivalent to [[a-zA-Z_0-9]]. With the [UNICODE_CHARACTER_CLASS] option (see below), it also recognizes accented letters
    [\W]
    matches any character that is not a word character
    [\num]
    num is a positive integer: refers to group number num. For example, [(.)\1] corresponds to two consecutive identical characters
    [\xnn], [\unnnn]
    corresponds to the hexadecimal character nn (2 digits) or nnnn (4 digits). For example, [\x41] corresponds to A

    An element in a template can appear once or multiple times. Let’s look at a few examples using the symbol [\d], which represents a single digit:

    template
    Meaning
    [\d]
    one digit
    [\d?]
    0 or 1 digit
    [\d*]
    0 or more digits
    [\d+]
    1 or more digits
    [\d{2}]
    2 digits
    [\d{3,}]
    At least 3 digits
    [\d{5,7}]
    between 5 and 7 digits

    Now let’s imagine a model capable of describing the expected format for a string:

    target string
    pattern
    a date in dd/mm/yy format
    [\d{2}/\d{2}/\d{2}]
    a time in the hh:mm:ss format
    [\d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}]
    an unsigned integer
    [\d+]
    a sequence of spaces, which may be empty
    [\s*]
    an unsigned integer that may be preceded or followed by spaces
    [\s*\d+\s*]
    an integer that may be signed and preceded or followed by spaces
    [\s*[+-]?\s*\d+\s*]
    an unsigned real number that may be preceded or followed by spaces
    [\s*\d+(\.\d*)?\s*]
    a real number that may be signed and preceded or followed by spaces
    [\s*[+-]?\s*\d+(\.\d*)?\s*]
    a string containing the word "just"
    [\bjuste\b]

    Note that within square brackets, the character [|] has no specific meaning: the [[+|-]] pattern, which is sometimes used for the sign, also accepts the character | before a number. Similarly, the decimal point must be escaped, [\.]: an unescaped period matches any character.

    You can specify where to search for the pattern in the string:

    pattern
    meaning
    [^modèle]
    the pattern starts the string
    [modèle$]
    Model ends the string
    [^modèle$]
    The pattern starts and ends the string
    [modèle]
    The pattern is searched for anywhere in the string, starting from the beginning of the string
    search string
    pattern
    a string ending with an exclamation point
    [!$]
    a string ending with a period
    [\.$]
    a string beginning with the sequence //
    [^//]
    a string consisting of a single word, possibly preceded or followed by spaces
    [^\s*\w+\s*$]
    a string consisting of exactly two words, possibly preceded or followed by spaces
    [^\s*\w+\s+\w+\s*$]
    a string containing the word "secret"
    [\bsecret\b]

    Sub sets of a pattern can be “extracted.” Thus, not only can we verify that a string matches a particular pattern, but we can also extract from that string the elements corresponding to the pattern’s sub sets that have been enclosed in parentheses. For example, if we parse a string containing a date in the format dd/mm/yy and also want to extract the elements dd, mm, and yy from that date, we would use the pattern [(\d\d)/(\d\d)/(\d\d)].

    In Java code, a pattern is written as a regular string: each character [\] in the pattern must be duplicated. The pattern [\d+] is written as ["\\d+"], and the pattern [\\], which represents the \ character, is written as ["\\\\"]. Text blocks do not change this: [\] is also an escape character here. The editor makes it easier to read: IntelliJ IDEA recognizes the strings passed to [Pattern.compile], highlights them as regular expressions, and allows you to test them.

    5.8.1. Check whether a string matches a given pattern

    A template is first compiled into a [java.util.regex.Pattern] object, which then provides [Matcher] objects responsible for searching within a given string:

    method
    role
    [static Pattern compile(String regex)]
    compiles the [regex] template; throws a [PatternSyntaxException] exception if the template is invalid
    [static Pattern compile(String regex, int flags)]
    same as above, with options (see below)
    [Matcher matcher(CharSequence input)]
    returns a [Matcher] object that looks up the template in [input]
    [boolean find()] (class [Matcher])
    searches for the next occurrence of the pattern in the string; returns [true] if one is found
    [boolean matches()] (class [Matcher])
    returns [true] if the entire string matches the pattern
    [static boolean matches(String regex, CharSequence input)]
    compiles the pattern and checks whether the entire string matches it

    // Check that a string matches a pattern
void main() {
    String modele1 = "^\\s*\\d+\\s*$";
    Pattern regex1 = Pattern.compile(modele1);
     // compare instances to the template
    for (String exemplaire : List.of("  123  ", "  123a  ", "4567")) {
        if (regex1.matcher(exemplaire).find()) {
            IO.println("[" + exemplaire + "] correspond au modèle [" + modele1 + "]");
        } else {
            IO.println("[" + exemplaire + "] ne correspond pas au modèle [" + modele1 + "]");
        }
    }
     // `find` searches for the pattern in the string; `matches` requires the entire string to match
    Pattern nombre = Pattern.compile("\\d+");
    IO.println("find(\"abc 123\") : " + nombre.matcher("abc 123").find()
            + ", matches(\"abc 123\") : " + nombre.matcher("abc 123").matches());
     // the static method Pattern.matches and the String.matches method: the entire string
    IO.println("Pattern.matches(date, \"18/05/97\") : "
            + Pattern.matches("\\d{2}/\\d{2}/\\d{2}", "18/05/97"));
    IO.println("\"5/1/01\".matches(date) : " + "5/1/01".matches("\\d{2}/\\d{2}/\\d{2}"));
}

    • line 3: the pattern for an unsigned integer, possibly surrounded by spaces, which occupies the entire string (anchors [^] and [$]). The [\] entries are duplicated;
    • line 4: the template compilation;
    • line 7: [find] searches for the pattern in the string. The string “123a,” surrounded by spaces, does not match the pattern: the character “a” cannot be a digit or a space. Without the anchors [^] and [$], the string would match, since it contains a number;
    • lines 14–16: the difference between [find], which searches for the pattern within the string, and [matches], which requires that the entire string match the pattern, as if it were bounded by [^] and [$];
    • Lines 18–20: The static method [Pattern.matches] and the method [matches] of the class [String] also test the entire string. They compile the pattern on every call: while useful for a standalone test, they should be avoided in a loop. The method [split] of [String], which we’ve already encountered, likewise compiles its pattern on every call, except for separators consisting of a single ordinary character, which it processes without a regular expression.

    5.8.2. Finding all occurrences of a pattern in a string

    The [find] method of a [Matcher] object can be called multiple times: each call searches for the next occurrence of the pattern. After a successful call, the [Matcher] object provides information about the occurrence found:

    • [group()]: the text of the occurrence, i.e., an element matching the pattern;
    • [start()]: the position where the element was found in the searched string; [end()]: the position following the element.

    // find all occurrences of a pattern in a string
void main() {
    String modele2 = "\\d+";
    Pattern regex2 = Pattern.compile(modele2);
    String exemplaire3 = "  123  456  789 ";
    IO.println("Modèle=[" + modele2 + "], exemplaire=[" + exemplaire3 + "]");
     // `find` moves from one occurrence to the next
    Matcher matcher = regex2.matcher(exemplaire3);
    int nbOccurrences = 0;
    while (matcher.find()) {
        nbOccurrences++;
        IO.println("[" + matcher.group() + "] trouvé en position " + matcher.start());
    }
    IO.println("Il y a " + nbOccurrences + " occurrences du modèle dans l'exemplaire");
     // results (Java 9): the stream of occurrences, to which the API Stream is applied
    int somme = regex2.matcher(exemplaire3).results().mapToInt(m -> Integer.parseInt(m.group())).sum();
    IO.println("somme des nombres trouvés : " + somme);
    long voyelles = Pattern.compile("[aeiouy]").matcher("anticonstitutionnellement").results().count();
    IO.println("nombre de voyelles de \"anticonstitutionnellement\" : " + voyelles);
}

    // retrieve parts of a pattern: groups
void main() {
    String modele3 = "(\\d\\d):(\\d\\d):(\\d\\d)";
    Pattern regex3 = Pattern.compile(modele3);
    String exemplaire4 = "Il est 18:05:49";
     // find searches for the first occurrence of the pattern
    Matcher resultat = regex3.matcher(exemplaire4);
    if (resultat.find()) {
        IO.println("L'exemplaire [" + exemplaire4 + "] correspond au modèle [" + modele3 + "]");
         // Parentheses groups are displayed; group 0 is the entire occurrence
        for (int i = 0; i <= resultat.groupCount(); i++) {
            IO.println("groupes[" + i + "]=[" + resultat.group(i) + "] trouvé en position "
                    + resultat.start(i));
        }
    } else {
        IO.println("L'exemplaire [" + exemplaire4 + "] ne correspond pas au modèle [" + modele3 + "]");
    }

     // named groups: (?<name>...)
    Pattern regexDate = Pattern.compile("(?<jour>\\d{1,2})/(?<mois>\\d{1,2})/(?<annee>\\d{4})");
    String texte = "Rendez-vous le 3/10/2026, puis le 15/11/2026.";
    DateTimeFormatter format = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("EEEE d MMMM yyyy");
    Matcher m = regexDate.matcher(texte);
    while (m.find()) {
         // A group is referred to by its name rather than its number
        int jour = Integer.parseInt(m.group("jour"));
        int mois = Integer.parseInt(m.group("mois"));
        int annee = Integer.parseInt(m.group("annee"));
        LocalDate date = LocalDate.of(annee, mois, jour);
        IO.println("[" + m.group() + "] : jour=" + jour + ", mois=" + mois + ", année=" + annee + " -> "
                + date.format(format));
    }

     // replaceAll: groups can be reused in the replacement string
    String inverse = regexDate.matcher(texte).replaceAll("${annee}-${mois}-${jour}");
    IO.println("replaceAll(chaîne) : " + inverse);
     // replaceAll with a function (Java 9): the replacement is calculated for each occurrence
    String iso = regexDate.matcher(texte).replaceAll(r -> LocalDate.of(Integer.parseInt(r.group(3)),
            Integer.parseInt(r.group(2)), Integer.parseInt(r.group(1))).toString());
    IO.println("replaceAll(fonction) : " + iso);
}

    • lines 7–8: the string [exemplaire4] is compared to the pattern [regex3]; [find] searches for the first occurrence of the pattern. After a successful call, we use two new methods from [Matcher]:
      • [groupCount] (line 11): the number of parenthesis groups in the pattern;
      • [group(i)] (line 12): the text captured by group #i; [group(0)], or [group()], is the entire occurrence of the pattern. [start(i)] is the position of this text in the parsed string. The loop therefore runs from 0 to [groupCount], inclusive;
    • line 20: a group can be named using the syntax [(?<nom>...)]. Here, the pattern recognizes a date in the format d/m/yyyy, with a one- or two-digit day and month;
    • lines 26–28: A named group is referred to by its name rather than its number: the code is more readable and does not depend on the order of the parentheses;
    • lines 29–31: The class [LocalDate] (Java 8) represents a date without a time. It is displayed using the template [EEEE d MMMM yyyy]: the day of the week appears in French;
    • line 35: the [replaceAll] method replaces each occurrence of the template with a string in which [${nom}] (or [$1], [$2]… for numbered groups) denotes the value of a group. Dates are thus rewritten in year-month-day format;
    • lines 38–39: an overloaded version of [replaceAll] (Java 9) takes a function that calculates the replacement text from each occurrence, of type [MatchResult]. Here, the date is constructed and replaced with its standardized notation ISO 8601, which is returned by the [toString] method of [LocalDate]: days and months always have two digits.

    // A program for learning regular expressions
void main() {
    while (true) {
         // the pattern is requested
        String modele = lire("Tapez le modèle à tester ou rien pour arrêter : ");
         // Done?
        if (modele.isBlank()) {
            break;
        }
         // Compiling the regular expression; an incorrect pattern causes an exception
        Pattern regex;
        try {
            regex = Pattern.compile(modele);
        } catch (PatternSyntaxException e) {
            IO.println("Erreur : " + e.getDescription() + " (position " + e.getIndex() + ")");
            continue;
        }
         // The examples to be compared against the pattern are requested
        while (true) {
            String chaine = lire("Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [" + modele
                    + "] ou rien pour arrêter : ");
             // Done?
            if (chaine.isBlank()) {
                break;
            }
            try {
                 // Performing the comparison, with a one-second time limit
                Matcher m = regex.matcher(new ChaineLimitee(chaine, Duration.ofSeconds(1)));
                boolean trouve = false;
                while (m.find()) {
                    trouve = true;
                     // The element matching the pattern is displayed
                    IO.println("J'ai trouvé la correspondance [" + m.group() + "] en position ["
                            + m.start() + "]");
                     // and its subelements (groups 1, 2, ...)
                    for (int j = 1; j <= m.groupCount(); j++) {
                        IO.println("    sous-élément [" + m.group(j) + "] en position ["
                                + m.start(j) + "]");
                    }
                }
                if (!trouve) {
                    IO.println("Je n'ai pas trouvé de correspondances");
                }
            } catch (DelaiDepasseException e) {
                IO.println("La recherche a été abandonnée : elle durait plus d'une seconde");
            }
        }
    }
}

// read a line from the keyboard; "" at the end of the stream
String lire(String invite) {
    String ligne = IO.readln(invite);
    return ligne == null ? "" : ligne;
}

// a string that cannot be read past a deadline
record ChaineLimitee(CharSequence texte, long limite) implements CharSequence {

    ChaineLimitee(CharSequence texte, Duration delai) {
        this(texte, System.nanoTime() + delai.toNanos());
    }

    @Override
    public char charAt(int index) {
         // the regular expression engine reads the string character by character
        if (System.nanoTime() > limite) {
            throw new DelaiDepasseException();
        }
        return texte.charAt(index);
    }

    @Override
    public int length() {
        return texte.length();
    }

    @Override
    public CharSequence subSequence(int debut, int fin) {
        return new ChaineLimitee(texte.subSequence(debut, fin), limite);
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return texte.toString();
    }
}

// the exception thrown when the timeout is exceeded (static: usable in the record)
static class DelaiDepasseException extends RuntimeException {
    @Serial
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
}

    • line 13: compilation of the pattern entered via the keyboard. An incorrect pattern triggers an exception [PatternSyntaxException], for which [getDescription] returns the error description and [getIndex] returns its position in the pattern (line 15). Its full message, rendered by [getMessage], spans several lines and shows the template with a marker below the error;
    • line 28: the search is not performed directly on the typed string, but on an object [ChaineLimitee] (lines 58–87), which limits the search duration to one second: if the search takes longer, a [DelaiDepasseException] exception is thrown and then caught on line 44. We’ll see later why this is useful and how it works;
    • lines 36–39: for each match, groups #1 and subsequent groups are displayed, if any;
    • lines 52–55: Unlike previous programs, spaces are not removed from the entered line; they may be part of the pattern or the string to be tested.

    The templates [^\s*\d+\s*$] and [^\s*(\d+)\s*$] demonstrate the benefits of using groups: the first recognizes the string “1456” preceded by three spaces, including the spaces; the second also extracts the number without the spaces. The [^(a+)+$] and [^(a+)+\1$] templates are discussed below.

    5.8.5. The split method

    We have already encountered the [split] method of the [String] class, whose separator is a regular expression. The [Pattern] class has the same method, which uses the precompiled pattern:

    method
    role
    [String[] split(CharSequence input)]
    The string [input] is split into fields, which are separated by a separator corresponding to the template
    [Stream<String> splitAsStream(CharSequence input)]
    same as above, but the fields are rendered as a stream

    Suppose, for example, that a text file contains lines of the form field1, field2, ..., fieldn. The fields are separated by a comma, but this comma may be preceded or followed by spaces. The template [\s*,\s*] describes this separator exactly, as shown by the program [Regex05.java]:

    // split: the separator is defined by a pattern
void main() {
    String ligne = "abc  , def  ,ghi ,   jkl";
     // a comma preceded and followed by any number of spaces
    Pattern separateur = Pattern.compile("\\s*,\\s*");
    String[] champs = separateur.split(ligne);
    for (int i = 0; i < champs.length; i++) {
        IO.println("champs[" + i + "]=[" + champs[i] + "]");
    }
     // multiple possible separators: ; or | or a sequence of spaces
    String[] mots = "un;deux|trois   quatre".split("[;|]|\\s+");
    IO.println("mots=" + Arrays.toString(mots));
     // splitAsStream: fields in the form of a stream
    IO.println("splitAsStream : " + separateur.splitAsStream(ligne).map(String::toUpperCase).toList());
}

    5.8.6. Precompiled templates, options, and searches that take too long

    Unlike other platforms, Java does not have a mechanism that generates the code for a regular expression search at program compile time: a pattern is always parsed at runtime by [Pattern.compile]. This compilation comes at a cost; therefore, best practice is to compile each known pattern once and for all in advance and store the [Pattern] object in a constant, as the program [Regex06.java] does. A [Pattern] object is immutable and can be used simultaneously by multiple threads; a [Matcher] object, which stores the state of a search, cannot.

    // templates compiled once and for all, options, protection against overly long searches

// one hour hh:mm:ss with named groups
static final Pattern HEURE = Pattern.compile("(?<h>\\d\\d):(?<m>\\d\\d):(?<s>\\d\\d)");
// yes, regardless of case
static final Pattern OUI = Pattern.compile("^\\s*oui\\s*$", Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE);
// a pathological pattern: a repeated group followed by a backreference to that group
static final Pattern CATASTROPHE = Pattern.compile("^(a+)+\\1$");

void main() {
     // 1 - patterns compiled only once, stored in constants
    IO.println("HEURE.matcher(\"Il est 18:05:49\").find() : " + HEURE.matcher("Il est 18:05:49").find());
    Matcher m = HEURE.matcher("départ à 07:45:00");
    if (m.find()) {
        IO.println("heures=" + m.group("h") + ", minutes=" + m.group("m") + ", secondes=" + m.group("s"));
    }

     // 2 - options: here, CASE_INSENSITIVE, set when the pattern is compiled
    for (String reponse : List.of("oui", "OUI", "Oui", "non", "ouiii")) {
        IO.print(reponse + "=" + OUI.matcher(reponse).matches() + " ");
    }
    IO.println();
     // MULTILINE: ^ and $ correspond to the beginning and end of each line; \w only recognizes [a-zA-Z0-9_]
    String texte = "prix: 10\nquantité: 3\ntotal: 30";
    affiche(Pattern.compile("^(\\w+): (\\d+)$", Pattern.MULTILINE), texte);
     // UNICODE_CHARACTER_CLASS: \w also recognizes accented letters
    affiche(Pattern.compile("^(\\w+): (\\d+)$", Pattern.MULTILINE | Pattern.UNICODE_CHARACTER_CLASS), texte);
     // options can also be written in the pattern: (?i) for CASE_INSENSITIVE, (?m) for MULTILINE
    IO.println("(?i)oui sur \"OUI\" : " + "OUI".matches("(?i)oui"));

     // 3 - a pattern with catastrophic backtracking, first without and then with a time limit
    for (int n : new int[]{10, 15, 20}) {
        String chaine = "a".repeat(n) + "!";
        long debut = System.nanoTime();
        boolean trouve = CATASTROPHE.matcher(chaine).find();
        IO.println(n + " a : " + trouve + " en " + (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000 + " ms");
    }
    String chaine = "a".repeat(30) + "!";
    try {
        IO.println(CATASTROPHE.matcher(new ChaineLimitee(chaine, Duration.ofMillis(100))).find());
    } catch (DelaiDepasseException e) {
        IO.println("30 a : " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : recherche abandonnée au bout de 100 ms");
    }
     // The Java engine recognizes the pattern (a+)+ without a backreference and responds immediately
    long debut = System.nanoTime();
    boolean trouve = Pattern.compile("^(a+)+$").matcher(chaine).find();
    IO.println("^(a+)+$ sur 30 a : " + trouve + ", réponse en moins d'une seconde : "
            + ((System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000 < 1000));
}

// display of name=value pairs found in a text
void affiche(Pattern modele, String texte) {
    Matcher ligne = modele.matcher(texte);
    while (ligne.find()) {
        IO.print("[" + ligne.group(1) + "=" + ligne.group(2) + "] ");
    }
    IO.println();
}

// A string that refuses to be read past a timeout
record ChaineLimitee(CharSequence texte, long limite) implements CharSequence {

    ChaineLimitee(CharSequence texte, Duration delai) {
        this(texte, System.nanoTime() + delai.toNanos());
    }

    @Override
    public char charAt(int index) {
        if (System.nanoTime() > limite) {
            throw new DelaiDepasseException();
        }
        return texte.charAt(index);
    }

    @Override
    public int length() {
        return texte.length();
    }

    @Override
    public CharSequence subSequence(int debut, int fin) {
        return new ChaineLimitee(texte.subSequence(debut, fin), limite);
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return texte.toString();
    }
}

// The exception thrown when the time limit is exceeded
static class DelaiDepasseException extends RuntimeException {
    @Serial
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
}

^(a+)+$ sur 30 a : false, réponse en moins d'une seconde : true

    Comments:

    • lines 4–8: The program’s templates are compiled once and stored in [static final] constants (Chapter 4), written in uppercase as is customary. In a compact source file, these constants are fields of the implicit class that contains the file’s methods;
    • lines 12–16: The constants are used in the same way as the [Pattern] objects in the previous programs;
    • line 6: the second parameter of [compile] is a combination of options. [CASE_INSENSITIVE] is case-insensitive: “OUI” and “Yes” match the pattern (line 4 of the results);
    • Lines 23–27: The options are combined with the operator [|]. [MULTILINE] matches [^] and [$] at the beginning and end of each line in the string, rather than just at the beginning and end of the string itself. However, with the default options, [\w] recognizes only unaccented letters: the line “quantity: 3” is not recognized (line 5 of the results). The option [UNICODE_CHARACTER_CLASS] (Java 7) assigns the correct Unicode meanings to [\w], [\d], [\s], and [\b]: accented letters are treated as word characters (line 6 of the results). This option should be used for all French text. Other useful options include: [DOTALL] ([.] also handles line breaks), [COMMENTS] (spaces in the template are ignored, allowing it to be written across multiple lines, with comments), [UNICODE_CASE] (along with [CASE_INSENSITIVE], this also ignores the case of accented letters: É and é);
    • line 29: options can also be written at the beginning of the template: [(?i)] for [CASE_INSENSITIVE], [(?m)] for [MULTILINE], [(?U)] for [UNICODE_CHARACTER_CLASS]…

    The rest of the program addresses a security issue. Some patterns are pathological: when applied to certain strings, they force the regular expression engine to try an enormous number of ways to match the string to the pattern before reaching a conclusion. The Java engine uses a process called “backtracking”: when an attempt fails, it returns to the last choice made and tries another one. The pattern [^(a+)+\1$] on line 8 is an example of this: When applied to a sequence of “a”s ending with another character, it tries every possible way to distribute the “a”s among the repetitions of the group and its backreference [\1] before concluding that the match has failed, and the number of possibilities multiplies with each additional “a.” This is known as a catastrophic backtracking. When applied to user-entered strings, such a pattern constitutes a security vulnerability (known as ReDoS, “regular expression denial of service”): just a few requests are enough to bring a server to a standstill.

    • Lines 32–37: The search duration is measured for 10, 15, and 20 a. It increases very rapidly (lines 8–10 of the results; durations vary from one execution and one machine to another). Since the duration roughly doubles with each additional a, the search would take several minutes with 30 a;
    • lines 38–43: The [Pattern] class has no timeout option. A standard technique is used: the search is performed in an object of type [ChaineLimitee] (lines 61–89), which implements the [CharSequence] interface accepted by [matcher]. The regular expression engine reads the string character by character using the [charAt] method: this method checks the time and throws a [DelaiDepasseException] exception (lines 92–95) if the deadline—stored when the object was created—has been exceeded. The search is abandoned after 100 ms;
    • lines 61–65: The [ChaineLimitee] record has two components: the text and the deadline, expressed as the value of the [System.nanoTime] clock, which must not be exceeded. The additional constructor calculates this deadline based on a timeout, an object [java.time.Duration];
    • line 92: The exception [DelaiDepasseException] is derived from [RuntimeException]: it is an unchecked exception that [charAt] can throw without declaring it. It is declared as [static] so that it can be created in the record, which is itself implicitly static. The field [serialVersionUID] prevents a compiler warning, since an exception is serializable;
    • lines 45–48: The Java runtime can recognize and efficiently handle simple cases of nested repetitions: the pattern [^(a+)+$], which is catastrophic with other runtimes, responds immediately here. It is the backward reference [\1] that prevents this optimization in the pattern on line 8.

    It is important to note that you should be wary of patterns containing nested repetitions ([(a+)+], [(\w+\s?)*]…) and limit the duration of searches as soon as the pattern or string being searched for comes from outside the program. Java’s possessive quantifiers ([a++], [a*+]), which prevent backtracking within the element they repeat, also allow you to write safe patterns, provided you fully understand their meaning.

    5.9. Example Application - V3

    We’ll revisit the application discussed in Chapter 3 (Version 1) and Chapter 4 (Version 2). Remember that this is an exercise: the tax scale used is the 2004 version (2003 income), which has remained unchanged since the original course.

    package impots;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.MathContext;

public abstract class AbstractImpot implements IImpot {

     // The tax brackets needed for the calculation come from an external source
     // known only to derived classes
    protected abstract TrancheImpot[] getTranchesImpot();

     // tax calculation
    @Override
    public int calculer(boolean marie, int nbEnfants, int salaire) {
         // Calculation of the number of shares
        BigDecimal nbParts = BigDecimal.valueOf(nbEnfants).divide(BigDecimal.TWO)
                .add(marie ? BigDecimal.TWO : BigDecimal.ONE);
        if (nbEnfants >= 3) {
            nbParts = nbParts.add(new BigDecimal("0.5"));
        }
         // Calculation of taxable income and the family quotient
        BigDecimal revenu = new BigDecimal("0.72").multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(salaire));
        BigDecimal quotient = revenu.divide(nbParts, MathContext.DECIMAL64);
         // Determination of the tax bracket: the last one is used if no other limit applies
        TrancheImpot[] tranches = getTranchesImpot();
        TrancheImpot tranche = tranches[tranches.length - 1];
        for (int i = 0; i < tranches.length - 1; i++) {
            if (quotient.compareTo(tranches[i].limite()) <= 0) {
                tranche = tranches[i];
                break;
            }
        }
         // tax calculation
        return revenu.multiply(tranche.coeffR()).subtract(nbParts.multiply(tranche.coeffN())).intValue();
    }
}

    The [calculer] method uses the tax brackets returned by the abstract method [getTranchesImpot] (line 10). The [AbstractImpot] class does not know where these brackets come from: it is up to the derived classes to provide them. In version 2, the derived class [HardwiredImpot] hard-coded them into its code. The calculations are performed using exact decimal numbers [java.math.BigDecimal] (Chapter 3): [BigDecimal.TWO] (Java 19) is the constant 2; the division of the revenue by the number of shares is performed with 16 significant digits ([MathContext.DECIMAL64]); and [intValue] returns the integer part of the result. A bracket is represented, as in version 2, by the record [TrancheImpot]:

    The new version stores the data in a file, which allows you to change the rate schedule without recompiling the program. We write two new classes derived from [AbstractImpot]:

    Numbers in the file are written with a decimal point. A data file must not depend on the language of the machine reading it: a file written with decimal commas and interpreted according to French rules ([NumberFormat.getInstance(Locale.FRANCE)]) would be rejected or, worse, misinterpreted on an English-language machine. The [new BigDecimal(String)] generator, like [Double.parseDouble], always expects a decimal point, regardless of the machine’s language. This is also the convention for JSON and most data formats.

    Processing these files may fail due to a missing file, a malformed line, an incorrect number, etc. We create a special exception class to report these errors, [ImpotException]. It will also be used for other data sources (the JSON file here, and databases later). It carries an error code:

    package impots;

import java.io.Serial;

// Exception thrown by the classes that read the tax brackets
// It derives from RuntimeException: this is an unchecked exception
public class ImpotException extends RuntimeException {

     // the class version for serialization (an exception is serializable)
    @Serial
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;

     // the error code (a combination of values CodeErreur)
    private final int code;

    public ImpotException(String message, int code) {
        super(message);
        this.code = code;
    }

    public ImpotException(String message, Throwable cause, int code) {
        super(message, cause);
        this.code = code;
    }

    public int getCode() {
        return code;
    }
}

    Comments:

    • Line 7: The [ImpotException] class derives from the [RuntimeException] class: this is an unchecked exception (Chapter 4). The compiler will not require the code that creates a [FileImpot] or [JsonImpot] object to catch this exception; that code will catch it where it is able to handle it;
    • Lines 10–11: Every exception is serializable by inheriting from the [Throwable] class. A serializable class should declare a version number [serialVersionUID], which is used to verify that a serialized object is deserialized by the same version of the class; otherwise, the compiler, when using the [-Xlint:all] option, issues a warning. The [@Serial] annotation (Java 14) indicates that the field is part of the serialization mechanism;
    • line 14: the error code, set when the exception is created;
    • lines 16–24: two constructors. The first takes an error message and a code; the second also takes the exception that caused the error (the cause), which will be accessible via the [getCause] method. It is this form of exception, with an integer code, that subsequent versions of the application will use.

    package impots;

import java.util.EnumSet;

// error codes: powers of 2, which can be combined
public enum CodeErreur {
    ACCES(1),       // The file cannot be read
    LIGNE(2),       // A row does not have three fields
    CHAMP1(4),      // Field 1 (limit) is incorrect
    CHAMP2(8),      // Field 2 (coeffR) is incorrect
    CHAMP3(16),     // Field 3 (coeffN) is incorrect
    JSON(32);       // The document JSON is incorrect

     // The integer value of the code
    private final int valeur;

    CodeErreur(int valeur) {
        this.valeur = valeur;
    }

    public int getValeur() {
        return valeur;
    }

     // the codes present in a code combination
    public static EnumSet<CodeErreur> decoder(int code) {
        EnumSet<CodeErreur> codes = EnumSet.noneOf(CodeErreur.class);
        for (CodeErreur c : values()) {
            if ((code & c.valeur) != 0) {
                codes.add(c);
            }
        }
        return codes;
    }
}

    Comments:

    • Lines 7–12: Possible error codes:
      • [ACCES]: error accessing the data file;
      • [LIGNE]: row missing the three expected fields, or file containing no time periods;
      • [CHAMP1], [CHAMP2], [CHAMP3]: Field 1, 2, or 3 in a row is incorrect;
      • [JSON]: The document JSON is incorrect;
    • Lines 15–23: A Java enum is a class; it can have fields, a (private) constructor, and methods. Each constant is constructed with its integer value, enclosed in parentheses;
    • lines 26–34: Some errors can occur in combination: all three fields in a line may be incorrect. Therefore, the error code values are powers of 2: each corresponds to a bit of the integer. An error in fields 2 and 3 will result in the code 8 | 16 = 24. The static method [decoder] performs the inverse operation: it converts the set of codes into an integer by testing each bit with the operator [&]. The result is a *[EnumSet]*, a specialized set for the constants of an enumeration, which stores them as the bits of an integer: this is the Java way of handling combinations of options. Its method [toString] displays a combination in the form “[CHAMP2, CHAMP3]”.

    package impots;

import java.io.BufferedReader;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;

// the tax brackets read from a text file of line limits:coeffR:coeffN
public class FileImpot extends AbstractImpot {

     // the field separator: the character : surrounded by optional spaces
    private static final Pattern SEPARATEUR = Pattern.compile("\\s*:\\s*");
     // a positive or zero number: digits, possibly followed by a period and digits
    private static final Pattern NOMBRE = Pattern.compile("\\d+(\\.\\d+)?");

     // the tax brackets read from the file
    private final TrancheImpot[] tranchesImpot;

     // Implementation of the parent class’s abstract method
    @Override
    protected TrancheImpot[] getTranchesImpot() {
        return tranchesImpot;
    }

    public FileImpot(String nomFichier) {
         // the filename (without the path) for error messages
        Path chemin = Path.of(nomFichier);
        String nom = chemin.getFileName().toString();
         // the tax brackets read; their number is unknown in advance
        List<TrancheImpot> tranches = new ArrayList<>();
        try (BufferedReader lecteur = Files.newBufferedReader(chemin)) {
            int numLigne = 0;
            String ligneLue;
            while ((ligneLue = lecteur.readLine()) != null) {
                numLigne++;
                String ligne = ligneLue.strip();
                 // empty lines are ignored
                if (ligne.isEmpty()) {
                    continue;
                }
                 // the line must have three fields
                String[] champs = SEPARATEUR.split(ligne);
                if (champs.length != 3) {
                    throw new ImpotException("Ligne n° " + numLigne + " incorrecte (" + ligne + ")",
                            CodeErreur.LIGNE.getValeur());
                }
                 // three positive or zero decimal numbers, written with a decimal point
                int code = 0;
                if (!NOMBRE.matcher(champs[0]).matches()) code |= CodeErreur.CHAMP1.getValeur();
                if (!NOMBRE.matcher(champs[1]).matches()) code |= CodeErreur.CHAMP2.getValeur();
                if (!NOMBRE.matcher(champs[2]).matches()) code |= CodeErreur.CHAMP3.getValeur();
                if (code != 0) {
                    throw new ImpotException("Ligne n° " + numLigne + " incorrecte (" + ligne + ")", code);
                }
                 // the new tax bracket is stored
                tranches.add(new TrancheImpot(new BigDecimal(champs[0]), new BigDecimal(champs[1]),
                        new BigDecimal(champs[2])));
            }
        } catch (IOException e) {
             // File access error: wrap it in a ImpotException
            throw new ImpotException("Erreur lors de la lecture du fichier " + nom, e,
                    CodeErreur.ACCES.getValeur());
        }
         // At least one tax bracket is required
        if (tranches.isEmpty()) {
            throw new ImpotException("Le fichier " + nom + " ne contient aucune tranche",
                    CodeErreur.LIGNE.getValeur());
        }
         // Transfer the list to the tax bracket array
        tranchesImpot = tranches.toArray(TrancheImpot[]::new);
    }
}

    Comments:

    • line 13: the class [FileImpot] is derived from the class [AbstractImpot], just as the class [HardwiredImpot] was in version 2;
    • Lines 16–18: Two regular expressions, compiled once and for all and stored as constants: the field separator for a boundary line:coeffR:coeffN (the character [:], preceded and followed by any number of spaces), and a positive or zero number, consisting of digits possibly followed by a period and more digits;
    • lines 21–27: the read segments, returned by the method [getTranchesImpot], which implements the abstract method [AbstractImpot];
    • line 29: the constructor receives the name of the text file containing the data. Its role is to populate the [tranchesImpot] array;
    • line 32: the file name without its path, used in error messages. The constructor may indeed receive a full path, which does not need to be displayed to the user;
    • line 34: Reading a text file is sequential: the number of lines is not known until the entire file has been read. Therefore, the array cannot be sized in advance; the chunks are temporarily stored in a list;
    • Lines 35–38: The file is read line by line using a [BufferedReader], opened by a [try] statement with resources;
    • lines 46–50: The line is split into fields using a regular expression; if there are not three fields, a [ImpotException] exception with code [LIGNE] is immediately thrown. The file is closed regardless: the [try] statement with resources closes [BufferedReader] regardless of how the block is exited—whether normally or via an exception;
    • Lines 52–58: validation of the three fields. Errors are accumulated in the variable [code] using the operator [|=], then reported collectively. The method [matches] requires that the integer field conform to the pattern [NOMBRE]: no sign, no spaces, and no decimal point. Negative numbers are thus rejected, which validates the data at the same time it is being checked;
    • lines 60–61: the fields, now validated, are converted to [BigDecimal], with a decimal point regardless of the machine’s language;
    • Lines 63–67: File access errors ([IOException] and its variants, such as [NoSuchFileException] for a missing file, [AccessDeniedException] for insufficient permissions, or [MalformedInputException] for a file that is not in UTF-8) are wrapped in a [ImpotException] with code [ACCES], with the original exception becoming its cause. The [ImpotException] exceptions thrown within the loop are not [IOException] exceptions: they are not intercepted by this [catch] clause and exit the constructor as-is;
    • lines 69–74: an empty file is rejected; otherwise, the list is transferred to the slice array, which was the purpose of the constructor.

    Encapsulating low-level exceptions ([IOException]) into an application-specific exception ([ImpotException]) allows the calling code to handle only one type of exception, regardless of the data source: a text file, a JSON file, and, later in the course, a database. This is also why [ImpotException] is unchecked: a checked exception would need to be declared by every method it passes through, which would tie the calling code to the details of the data source.

    package impots;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.Arrays;
import tools.jackson.core.JacksonException;
import tools.jackson.databind.json.JsonMapper;

// the tax brackets read from a file JSON
public class JsonImpot extends AbstractImpot {

     // The JsonMapper is reusable and can be used by multiple threads: only one is created
    private static final JsonMapper MAPPER = JsonMapper.builder().build();

     // the tax brackets read from the file
    private final TrancheImpot[] tranchesImpot;

     // Implementation of the parent class’s abstract method
    @Override
    protected TrancheImpot[] getTranchesImpot() {
        return tranchesImpot;
    }

    public JsonImpot(String nomFichier) {
         // the file name, without its path, for error messages
        Path chemin = Path.of(nomFichier);
        String nom = chemin.getFileName().toString();
        String json;
        try {
             // reading the file
            json = Files.readString(chemin);
        } catch (IOException e) {
            throw new ImpotException("Erreur lors de la lecture du fichier " + nom, e,
                    CodeErreur.ACCES.getValeur());
        }
        TrancheImpot[] tranches;
        try {
             // deserialization of the tax bracket array
            tranches = MAPPER.readValue(json, TrancheImpot[].class);
        } catch (JacksonException e) {
            throw new ImpotException("Le fichier " + nom + " est incorrect : " + e.getOriginalMessage()
                    + " (ligne " + e.getLocation().getLineNr() + ", colonne " + e.getLocation().getColumnNr()
                    + ")", e, CodeErreur.JSON.getValeur());
        }
         // At least one slice is required; negative values are not allowed
        if (tranches == null || tranches.length == 0) {
            throw new ImpotException("Le fichier " + nom + " ne contient aucune tranche",
                    CodeErreur.JSON.getValeur());
        }
        if (Arrays.stream(tranches).anyMatch(t -> negatif(t.limite()) || negatif(t.coeffR())
                || negatif(t.coeffN()))) {
            throw new ImpotException("Le fichier " + nom + " contient une valeur négative ou absente",
                    CodeErreur.JSON.getValeur());
        }
        tranchesImpot = tranches;
    }

     // A missing (null) or negative value is invalid
    private static boolean negatif(BigDecimal valeur) {
        return valeur == null || valeur.signum() < 0;
    }
}

    Comments:

    • Line 15: A single [JsonMapper], stored in a constant, is used for all [JsonImpot] objects. The properties JSON, [limite], [coeffR], and [coeffN] are named after the components of the [TrancheImpot] record: no annotation is necessary;
    • lines 31–37: reading the file; an access error is handled as in [FileImpot];
    • line 41: a single instruction converts the text JSON into an array of slices. Jackson constructs each record by calling its constructor and converts the numbers JSON to [BigDecimal] without any loss of precision;
    • lines 42–46: an invalid document causes a [JacksonException], encapsulated in a [ImpotException] with code [JSON]. The message indicates the location of the error, identified by [getLocation];
    • lines 48–56: deserialization checks the document’s format, not the validity of the data: it remains to be verified that there is at least one segment (the document [null] or [[]] is a valid JSON) and that no values are negative or missing. If a property is missing from a JSON object, the corresponding component is assigned the value [null]. The [anyMatch] operation of the API Stream performs this final check in a single statement, with [Arrays.stream(tranches)] returning the stream of array elements;
    • lines 61–63: the method that tests a value.

    Comparing the two classes is instructive: with a structured data format and a library that understands it, parsing the file requires almost no code.

    package impots;

// Tax calculation, version 3: tax brackets are read from a file
// Syntax: mvn exec:java [-Dexec.args="fichier"]; file: DataImpot.txt by default, or a .json file
public class Main {

    private static final String SYNTAXE = """
            syntaxe : Marié NbEnfants Salaire
            Marié : o pour marié, n pour non marié
            NbEnfants : nombre d'enfants
            Salaire : salaire annuel en euros""";

    public static void main(String[] args) {
         // the data file is searched for in the current folder
        String nomFichier = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "DataImpot.txt";
        IO.println("Tranches d'impôt lues dans [" + nomFichier + "]");

         // creation of a IImpot object; the class depends on the file extension
        IImpot impot;
        try {
            String extension = nomFichier.substring(nomFichier.lastIndexOf('.') + 1).toLowerCase();
            impot = switch (extension) {
                case "json" -> new JsonImpot(nomFichier);
                default -> new FileImpot(nomFichier);
            };
        } catch (ImpotException e) {
             // displaying the error; the code is displayed as a set of CodeErreur
            String origine = e.getCause() == null ? ""
                    : ", Exception d'origine : " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName();
            IO.println("L'erreur suivante s'est produite : [Code=" + CodeErreur.decoder(e.getCode())
                    + ", Message=" + e.getMessage() + origine + "]");
             // program termination
            System.exit(1);
            return;
        }

         // input loop
        while (true) {
             // Tax calculation parameters are requested
            String saisie = IO.readln("Paramètres du calcul de l'impôt au format : "
                    + "Marié (o/n) NbEnfants Salaire ou rien pour arrêter : ");
            String parametres = saisie == null ? "" : saisie.strip();
             // Is there anything to do?
            if (parametres.isEmpty()) {
                break;
            }
             // Checking the number of fields in the entered row
            String[] champs = parametres.split("\\s+");
            if (champs.length != 3) {
                IO.println(SYNTAXE);
                continue;
            }
             // Checking parameter validity
             // married
            String marie = champs[0].toLowerCase();
            if (!marie.equals("o") && !marie.equals("n")) {
                IO.println(SYNTAXE + "\nArgument marié incorrect : tapez o ou n");
                continue;
            }
             // nbEnfants
            int nbEnfants = entier(champs[1]);
            if (nbEnfants < 0) {
                IO.println(SYNTAXE + "\nArgument NbEnfants incorrect : tapez un entier positif ou nul");
                continue;
            }
             // salary
            int salaire = entier(champs[2]);
            if (salaire < 0) {
                IO.println(SYNTAXE + "\nArgument salaire incorrect : tapez un entier positif ou nul");
                continue;
            }
             // The parameters are correct: the tax is calculated
            IO.println("Impôt=" + impot.calculer(marie.equals("o"), nbEnfants, salaire) + " euros");
        }
    }

     // a positive integer or zero; -1 if the string is not an integer
    private static int entier(String champ) {
        try {
            return Integer.parseInt(champ);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            return -1;
        }
    }
}

    Comments:

    • lines 7–11: the help text, in a text block stored in a constant;
    • Line 15: The name of the data file is passed as an argument; by default, it is [DataImpot.txt]. With Maven, the program’s arguments are passed via the property [exec.args]: [mvn exec:java -Dexec.args="DataImpot.json"];
    • Lines 21–25: An expression [switch] (Chapter 3) selects the class to instantiate based on the file extension, which is extracted from the filename using [lastIndexOf] and [substring]. The two branches return objects of different types, [JsonImpot] and [FileImpot], both of type [IImpot]. The rest of the program only recognizes the [IImpot] interface and is unaware of where the data comes from;
    • lines 26–35: Creating the object may trigger a [ImpotException], which is displayed before the program terminates. The code is decoded into a set of [CodeErreur] messages to be displayed in plain text; the original exception, if any, is indicated by its type. The [return] statement following [System.exit] is never executed, but the compiler—which does not know that [System.exit] does not yield control—requires it: without it, the variable [impot] would not be considered initialized on line 73;
    • Lines 38–74: The dialog loop is the one from version 2.

Tranches d'impôt lues dans [DataImpotInvalide.json]
L'erreur suivante s'est produite : [Code=[JSON], Message=Le fichier DataImpotInvalide.json est incorrect : Cannot deserialize value of type `java.math.BigDecimal` from String "0,068": not a valid representation (ligne 3, colonne 31), Exception d'origine : InvalidFormatException]

    Jackson’s message specifies the error precisely: the string “0.068” cannot be converted to [BigDecimal]. Jackson accepts a string where a number is expected if it contains a valid number (“0.068”); it is the decimal point that is rejected. The error is located on line 3 of the document—Jackson numbers lines starting at 1—and in column 31, immediately after the incorrect value.

    5.10. Conclusion

    This chapter has introduced the Java classes used in almost all programs:

    • the immutable strings [String], which are compared with [equals] and not with [==], and [StringBuilder] for constructing them piece by piece; the formats [String.format] and [formatted], the text blocks;
    • tables and the [Arrays] class;
    • the [List] collections, [Map], [Set], [Deque], and their implementations [ArrayList], [HashMap], [LinkedHashMap], [TreeMap], [HashSet], [ArrayDeque], [PriorityQueue]; immutable collections ([List.of], [List.copyOf], [Collections.unmodifiableList]), Java 21 sequenced collections, and comparators ([Comparator]); Java 1.0 collections ([Vector], [Hashtable], [Stack]) are deprecated;
    • the API Stream, its intermediate and terminal operations, its collectors, and its lazy evaluation;
    • text files ([Files], [Path], [BufferedReader], [BufferedWriter]), still in UTF-8, binary files ([DataOutputStream], [DataInputStream], [RandomAccessFile]) and the JSON serialization using Jackson, which replaces the deprecated Java binary serialization;
    • regular expressions, compiled once and for all and protected against excessively long searches when processing external data.

    The sample application now reads its data from a text file or JSON. The following chapter reorganizes it into layers: data reading, tax calculation, and user interaction will become independent components.
